utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We're back here after a fairly long spell and I know you are very hard pressed to meet the deadline. I congratulate all of you for meeting it. That's excellent. Now, we have a few motions to consider. Some have been taken over by the efficiency of the machinery here. Perhaps the only one I can have in mind is Mrs. McMurrey's admission against the leading counsel for Mucic. Do you still think it is necessary to argue it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do believe that there needs to be an objection. I would like to, but of course, I am not going to reargue all of the points. Everything that I stated in my motion, I still stand for. Basically, that Ms. Buturovic was our investigator for a short period of time. As the Court is aware, there was a conflict in the fee vouchers. That Mr. Landzo signed a waiver to allow her to be investigator for Mr. Mucic, but he did not sign a waiver to allow her, saying that there was no conflict of interest if she were lead counsel. There is another thing I did not say in my motion. That she also represented two of our witnesses who we called here under subpoena who refused to testify, which also amounts to a conflict of interest, I believe. I don't believe that the Defence of Mr. Mucic will be prejudiced by her disqualification because Mr. Kuzmanovic is going to do all of the closing argument anyway. So he is there and present and would be qualified to represent Mr. Mucic in case the Court did decide to disqualify Ms. Buturovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, do you think merely making closing speeches, which did not entail any additional evidence, that all that has been recorded? Does is it make any difference to the case of Esad?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am not sure I am clear what the question is. I believe with the punishment -- if the verdict is guilty and if there is -- there is a lot of ifs -- if we go on to the punishment phase, that the knowledge that Ms. Buturovic has as our investigator and, you know, the conflict of interest that I think is rampant on her part because of the conflicts that she's had with us, would make a difference if it goes past the verdict, Your Honour. As far as closing argument goes, I don't see there could be much of a big conflict for closing argument, no. I think that was your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, actually, that was the area I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just one thing. We are to confine ourselves to what the evidence is before us at this stage. So whether Madam Buturovic had some knowledge, which she shouldn't bring to the Court isn't really relevant at this stage. At the earlier stage you could say. But at this stage we need to confine what the evidence is before us. Madam Buturovic was not so shaded with the defence of any of the accused at the evidence stage. It's merely a question of arguments now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The Court is absolutely correct. I believe at this point it would be very difficult for her to have a conflict of interest. But, in the future, if it goes to the sentencing/punishment stage and all evidence is relevant, then I believe there would be a conflict at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then you can raise a point at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that resolves it. We don't have to call you for any replies to the motion, so we'll leave it as it is. You are free to take notes in the closing arguments in the interest of your clients. Now, is there any outstanding motion? I think Mr. Moran's motion, as I said, need not keep us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour. The Appeals Chamber made that motion pretty moot this morning. The problem is solved. You're aware that my worry was I didn't know whether the Trial Chamber was deprived of jurisdiction because of the appeal. Well, the appeal is over. The Trial Chamber has been held to have ruled correctly. That's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am only interested that you are more interested in the state of the appellate himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, all I can say on that is I was thinking more along the lines of jurisdiction. I didn't want have the Trial Chamber and the Appellate Chamber dealing with the same case at the same time and trying to juggle who is doing what. That's why I brought it to everyone's attention. I am sure you know I brought it to everyone's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You did the right thing. Now, you've all received the schedule for argument and the procedure we intend to adopt. Then, do we call on the Prosecution to present its summary for our arguments.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution, appearing with Mr. Niemann, senior trial attorney, and Mr. Huber. Good morning to Defence counsel too. Your Honours, this Tribunal represents a precedent and a challenge. We are here as representatives of the international community to prosecute those persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law. We are to do so impartially without regard to ethnicity, without regard to politics and without regard to victor's justice. This Tribunal is to conduct a fair trial, one which searches for the truth while being fair to the parties, the victims, and of course, the accused themselves. After the trial, if the evidence has not established the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, it is certainly the duty of this Tribunal to acquit. But if the evidence has established the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, it is the duty of this Tribunal to convict. When this is done and when those persons proved to be responsible for violations of law are convicted, justice will have been achieved and this Tribunal will have met one of its fundamental challenges to show to the persons in the former Yugoslavia and the international community, generally, that even in war there are limits. That the principles of international law do mean something in this modern world and in modern warfare and that persons who violate those principles can be found responsible. Let's be honest, the challenge is not an easy one: practically, emotionally, legally. It's a hard, laborious process. It's especially hard here because not only is this Tribunal a precedent, but this trial is, itself, a precedent. This Tribunal will be rendering one of the first verdicts of command responsibility. Will be considering new issues regarding mental health. I am sure we will be considering many other issues as well. The challenge of finding the truth may not always be as easy as it is in our national systems. At the time the crimes happened, there was not an independent police force operating, rather there was a war going on. So some things, be they documents, autopsies, contemporaneous interviews, may not be in evidence. Many of these things never existed because of the ongoing war. Even when such physical evidence did exist, it may be gone or unavailable because it was destroyed after the war, because it's in the hands of persons in whose interest it is not to turn it over. So the evidence sometimes may take a slightly different form. Further, with respect to witnesses, sometimes it might be harder to have witnesses testify. Sometimes the witnesses can't be located or they're too traumatised or scared to testify. When the witnesses do come, there are language differences, maybe even some cultural differences to consider. But while the process of presenting and evaluating the evidence may take a little longer, require a little more work, the basic process is the same here as in all criminal trials. It is to evaluate the evidence, including the reasonable inferences to be drawn from the evidence. It is to evaluate the witnesses, including their credibility. In all of this, you will resort to your experience as jurists, as human beings and you will rely on your common sense. So the process may take a little longer or be a little harder, but it's fundamentally the same. Of course, the ultimate question is the same: Does the evidence establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt? When you consider the evidence in this case, Your Honours, as a whole, when you consider the physical evidence, the testimony of the witnesses, the inferences that must be drawn from the evidence, we respectfully submit that there can only be one conclusion. That is, that the evidence has established beyond a reasonable doubt, the guilt of each of the four accused in this case. In considering this case, I submit there are really two kinds of issues. One kind surrounding the crimes themselves and the second kind concerning responsibility for those crimes. Just for one minute I would like to talk to about the law as it regards to the crimes. The Prosecution submits that there can be no genuine dispute, that the underlying crimes charged here: murder, torture, rape; are crimes that are recognised by Articles 2 and 3 of our statute. We also submit there can't be any genuine dispute that Article 3 is applicable to this case. There is, however, a dispute about whether Article 2, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions is applicable. The defence would interpret the law narrowly so that it would, in effect, only apply in those situations, where long established countries are at war with each other with well-organised and well-dressed armies fighting each other. The Prosecution submits the world isn't always that simple. Countries break up and complicated questions of succession and reorganisation and recognition exist. Other countries become involved with different parts of the war. Citizenship laws don't always exist immediately. Even when they do, they're sometimes not clear or in accordance with international law. The parties on all the sides won't always have uniforms. But international humanitarian law, including as it has developed since the Second World War doesn't require the world to be that simple for the law to apply. The application of the Geneva Convention depends and looks to the reality of the situation. So someone doesn't necessarily have to wear a uniform to be entitled to POW status as long as they're in combat they wear their arms openly. Persons can be protected even where the internal, technical, citizenship requirements are not clear. Here, in this case, in the Celebici case, the reality of the situation as shown by the Prosecution evidence, and indeed, as acknowledged by the Defence witnesses and acknowledged by the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina upon whose behalf the accused were acting in 1992. The reality of the situation was that this was an international armed conflict and that persons in Celebici were arrested because they were considered to be Serbs and possible POWs associated with the adversary. Article 2 should, therefore, protect the victims in the Celebici camp. With respect to the underlying crime, Your Honours, you heard testimony from 30 detainees, 30 courageous people, 30 survivors, who came here from all over the world to tell you about what they experienced and about what they saw and heard of the experience of others. Some were in Celebici for as long as seven months. Many still bore the scars, emotional and physical, of their experience there. It's been a while since we've heard from the detainees and it's easy as we discuss the structure of the army, the strictures of the international law, the details of an accused's psychiatric history, it's easy not to think about the victims. In fact, it's often appropriate and sometimes even necessary to maintain a distance from the crimes. But we can't forget about the crimes or the victims entirely. When one remembers the testimony from the victims and thinks about it just for a minute, the crimes are there. The crimes, which is really the reason why we're all here. You heard from some of the victims. A woman who after being raped multiple times by persons young enough to be her son said she will never be the same. Numerous persons who have been set on fire. Persons who had lit fuses put in their anus. Persons who were forced to commit sex acts family members. People who were beaten to unconsciousness and people who were beaten so badly they couldn't walk for days. People who beaten so badly that they defecated in their single pair of pants. People who had to hear or watch as their fathers or their sons or their friends and neighbours were beaten, often beaten to death. Many of the incidents the victims told you about were particularly noteworthy because they were unusual in their details or in their savagery. The victims also told you about the ordinary incidents, things that happened every day, when they would be kicked in the ribs with army boots when they were sitting in the hangar in the required position. When they were hit with rifle butts when they ran to the open trench to try to go to defecate in their allotted several minutes. These things happen all the time. You also heard from the victims that all the time they were in a state of fear, even when they weren't actually being mistreated. They had to live every day and almost every moment in fear that they would be called out, called out, and beaten and raped or killed. One witness talked about how happy the detainees were once when there was a big rain and thunderstorm. How they actually slept soundly because they knew that no one was going to come and get them that night. You heard from a large number of victims and, as I said, some victims didn't testify for various reasons. Of course, there were also some victims who could not come: Scepo Gotovac, Zeljko Milosevic, Simo Jovanovic, Bosko Samoukovic, Slavko Susic, Milorad Kuljanin, Jelico Cecez, Slobodan Babic, Petko Gligorevic, Gojko Miljanic, Zeljko Klimenta, Miroslav Vujicic, Pero Mrkajic. You didn't get to hear from these victims because these victims were all dead, murdered in Celebici. The testimony from the detainees would be more than enough to prove the crimes charged. But, of course, you have more than that in this case. You have, for instance, testimony from persons who worked in the camp, including Witnesses D and T. You have the report made in June '92 by a group of Muslims and Croats who were supposed to work in the camp as an investigation commission, who finally refused to work because they didn't want to be a part of it. So they wrote a report. In that report they said that there were frequent murders. They said women were being taken out and sexually abused. They talked about the terrible beatings. It's all in there. Now the Prosecution and Defence can make their arguments about whether the persons to whom the report was directed, including Mr. Delalic, actually saw the report. But they can't honestly that dispute that in 1992 the crimes talked about in the report happened. And, of course, we can't forget that the accused themselves have told you that horrific crimes were happening. Mr. Landzo spoke to you directly about the mistreatment by himself and by others. In fact, he could only remember one other guard who didn't mistreat detainees. Mr. Delic in his OTP interview said that no night would go by without the prisoners being beaten. Mr. Mucic said in his interview that he heard reports from others that he saw the injuries and even that he, himself, saw people being abused. Even Mr. Delalic, who was not at the camp frequently, reported in his interview that from the beginning he knew about problems in Celebici, including that persons could come to beat the Serbs for revenge. Then later in August he heard from the Red Cross that persons, including Mr. Delic, were mistreating the prisoners. So in this case, Your Honours, there really isn't any doubt that there were crimes. As set out in detail in our written submissions, there really isn't any doubt that the crimes set out in the indictment were committed as alleged. So then we come to the responsibility issues. Because each one of the four accuses says, well, these victims have been murdered, tortured, otherwise mistreated, but I am not responsible. So let me briefly speak to the responsibility of each of the accused. Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo are charged under 7(1) of our Statute with direct participation in a number of crimes. Mr. Delic has denied committing any crimes at all. And our response to that is simply ask that the evidence be reviewed. The evidence is overwhelming that among other things, Mr. Delic murdered, Mr. Delic tortured, Mr. Delic raped, Mr. Delic beat and Mr. Delic humiliated detainees. The detainees tried to explain to us what it felt like, how they were terrified at the sight of him. In fact, everyone was terrified of him, the detainees and even the people who worked at the camp. As one detainee put it, he was God and your life depended on it. Mr. Delic revelled in this. He revelled in what he could do, and what he could do, he did do, and then he bragged about it. He used his baseball bat. He used to his boot. He used his rifle. He used a special electrical device. He used his sex and he used his power. He used all these things to mistreatment the prisoners themselves. Then he used his position as a deputy commander to order others to do the same things. A number of the detainees talked about hearing Mr. Delic order guards to mistreat detainees. And sometimes the detainees could actually watch Mr. Delic as he watched the mistreatment or they could hear him as he supervised and gave instructions. Mr. Delic killed, tortured, raped, beat, and what does the Defence suggest during the trial about Mr. Delic's activities in the camp? The Defence brought out that after a few months Mr. Delic got some blankets and divided them up so each detainee had part of a blanket. The detainee said, "Yes, that's true." Fine, later when sentencing Mr. Delic for murdering, raping and torturing, you can consider Mr. Delic once gave them part of a blanket. Mr. Landzo is charged with murders, tortures, really almost any kind of mistreatment that can be imagined, Mr. Landzo did it. His time in the camp was an orgy of sadism. Mr. Landzo agrees he committed many of these crimes, but he says he is not responsible. In fact, the Landzo Defence went so far as to claim, and I quote, "The true victim of the aggression in this case is Esad Landzo." If it wasn't so offensive it would be almost comical. We heard about him being pushed over by a goat, and his asthma, and his hand, and his friendship with stray dogs and his art school; and for all these reasons and more the Defence says Mr. Landzo has a personality disorder and post-traumatic stress syndrome, and so he has diminished responsibility. As a matter of fact and as a matter of law, the Prosecution respectfully submits that the submissions of the Defence should be summarily rejected. The Prosecution agrees Mr. Landzo has certain problems. Anyone who heard the testimony of the victims would know Mr. Landzo had some problems. We didn't need four psychiatrists to tell us that. But lots of people and lots of criminals have problems. The Defence points out Mr. Landzo was a young lad and easily influenced. Prosecution agrees Mr. Landzo was young, an adult, of course, but young, and easily influenced. But the evidence shows that he still had the ability to make his own decisions. And he did make his own decisions. Lots of people and lots of criminals are young and easily influenced. That isn't a defence to responsibility. There is nothing in Mr. Landzo's psychiatric history or any other history that would excuse him from responsibility or would serve to diminish his responsibility. There is no doubt Mr. Landzo knew the difference between right and wrong and he could control his actions. In fact, the evidence shows when it was in his interest to do so, Mr. Landzo easily controlled his actions. Mr. Landzo chose to follow orders to kill, torture and otherwise mistreat prisoners, and he chose to kill, torture and mistreat prisoners on his own initiative; and he is responsible for his choices. This is a man who told a defence psychiatrist that he would inflict pain and suffering on prisoners for two reasons: One, that he was ordered to do so; and two, because he was bored and frustrated. He stated he never had any difficulty doing this and that he enjoyed it. This is a man, Your Honours, who when asked by his own attorneys, did you mistreat a particular person, sometimes he said, "I did," sometimes he said, "I think I did, I think I set that person's leg on fire," and other times he says, "I can't remember." This is a man who did so many terrible things to so many different people he can't even remember them all. Your Honours, this is a man who needs to be made to take responsibility for his actions. So, the evidence establishes that Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo committed many crimes over many months, they did terrible things, and they need to be found guilty. But the next question is: How were they allowed to do these things? They and the many others who committed horrible crimes, how were they allowed to do it? How in an official military prison could so many crimes happen over so many months? How could it happen? Who let it happen? And that's another question of responsibility. The question of superior authority. And it's a question that's a big part of this case and a question that's a big part of why this Tribunal exists. Because it's a sad truth that people like Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo exist everywhere, and that's why there is a doctrine of superior authority. The law which says to superiors, you have responsibilities to find out what's going on and to prevent or punish crimes, even if you, yourself didn't participate in the crimes and even if you didn't order the crimes, even if you're a good person who didn't want the crimes to happen, even if you were busy with other important matters; if you are a superior, you have certain responsibilities. The exact nature of the responsibilities and what kind of action should be taken will depend on the circumstances, including the scope of the authority, the nature of the misconduct, the avenues available to prevent or punish. So what a superior is obligated to do may differ, but that they are obligated to do something is clear. Mr. Delic, Mr. Mucic, Mr. Delalic all say they weren't superiors. They more or less agree they didn't do anything to prevent or punish what was going on in the camp, but they say it wasn't their responsibility. Each of them says, "I was in some ways at some time involved in the administration of the camp, but I wasn't a superior." Mr. Delic says he was just a deputy commander with no authority. Mr. Mucic says he was just a commander or warden with no authority. Mr. Delalic says he was just a coordinator and Tactical Group commander who handled matters on other people's behalf, but he had no authority. The evidence, however, is to the contrary with respect to each of the three accused. First, Mr. Delic. The evidence shows that Mr. Delic had authority over the guards. And when Mr. Mucic was gone, as was frequently the case, Mr. Delic was in charge with full authority. He exercised his authority over the guards, but instead of preventing them from mistreating the prisoners, instead of punishing them, he chose to encourage them. It's possible Mr. Delic's authority was not entirely unfettered. It's possible he could not have instantly discharged a guard. But it is clear he could have taken any number of actions to prevent or punish; reassigning the guards, confining them to barracks, preventing them from contact with the detainees, notifying the superiors, recommending the guards be court-martialled, resigning. But what did he do? When asked if he ever advised his commander or others of what he had seen, he indicated no, and he said, "There was no rule. It wasn't important to anyone whether anyone would be beaten or killed." Mr. Mucic was commander in Celebici from almost the beginning of the camp's existence. He knew prisoners were mistreated, and the evidence suggests that sometimes he wanted them mistreated. Other times he may not have wanted it, but he didn't do anything to stop it. Maybe sometimes he intervened to help a friend, maybe he didn't like having the guards to mistreat prisoners when he was there to see it; but without any doubt he knew the prisoners were being mistreated, including when he wasn't there. And, of course, he wasn't there very much, and one reason he wasn't there at night, as he said in his interview, was because, "I was afraid of the guards in the camp, and for that reason I never slept in the camp." Three hundred persons or more were at the mercy of the guards and the commander is too scared to sleep there himself. And what did Mr. Mucic do? Nothing. He didn't take it seriously. In fact, it appears he doesn't take much seriously, and normally that's his own business; but when he was a superior, he had people's lives in his hands, and he was legally obligated to take his responsibility seriously, and he didn't. In his interview he was asked what he had done to prevent murders such as occurred when he was commander. And he said, "I have no answer to that question, nothing was done." Mr. Mucic may not take what happened seriously, Your Honours, but this Tribunal must. Mr. Delalic is a more complicated case of superior responsibility. Many of the victims were not in a position to see who was Mr. Mucic's superior. Mr. Mucic didn't testify, so we can't ask him as part of the trial testimony. So, it's true that the case is more complicated. I submit to you that this is entirely normal. It will be true in every case of command responsibility before this Tribunal. And the higher up the chain of command you go and the more intelligent, the more savvy the superior, the more complicated the evidence will be. It doesn't mean the evidence is any less convincing. It doesn't mean the evidence is not sufficient to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; but the picture may be more complicated. The Chamber has to look at a number of pieces of evidence in different testimonies and draw necessary inferences. And you have to look at evidence and fit it together. Is it consistent with each other or inconsistent? You have to use your common sense in determining what is reasonable and what is not. And it may well be that no one piece of evidence will convince you. It may be that for any one piece of evidence, or even more than one, other reasonable or even unreasonable but still plausible explanations exist. But the question is, when you put the pieces of evidence together, do they fit? Do they corroborate? Is there a reasonable explanation that could fit all the different pieces of evidence together? In this case, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that when you put all the evidence together, there is only one conclusion that may be drawn. The only reasonable conclusion that can be drawn from this evidence considered together is that Mr. Delalic was a superior authority regarding Celebici. In fact, let me say even more. This is an especially strong case of command responsibility. And in saying that, let me talk for a minute about what we have in this case. You have witness testimony and you have much more. You have orders, including orders from Mr. Delalic to Mr. Mucic. You have media interviews with Mr. Delalic in 1992. You have video-tapes, including video-tapes taken during 1992. You have reports from international organisations. You have documents from the army itself. You have release papers from the prisoners. You have numerous documents written by the accused himself concerning some of the issues in dispute. There have been and will be many command responsibility cases where only a few of these things exist, but here you have all of them. And this evidence, and all the other evidence that came out in the trial put together, establishes that Mr. Delalic was a superior. Some of the evidence may be -- some of the pieces of evidence may be small, some big, some may be direct, some may be circumstantial; but all of it fits together and leads to an inescapable conclusion, that Mr. Delalic was a superior. The Defence has offered explanations for much but not all the evidence, and the Prosecution suggests the explanations are incredible. We ask the Chamber to use its common sense. One might be able to accept one or two, but it is impossible, absolutely impossible that all these varied and different pieces of evidence from all different sources all pointing to one conclusion, it's impossible to believe they are the result of some unfortunate coincidence. It defies common sense. It defies even the imagination. The Defence suggests Mr. Delalic is playing dress up and pretending to be in command when he is shown in video exercising command. The Defence suggests the supreme command would have appointed Mr. Delalic to lead Tactical Group 1, tasked with lifting the siege of Sarajevo, the most important priority at the time. Even though, according to the Defence, he had been a civilian with no prior command position. Defence suggests that the order of appointment, which says he has certain authority and would be consistent with the importance of his task, doesn't mean what it says it means. The Defence suggests that different journalists, all of them made mistakes when they acted like he was commander or involved in Celebici. Defence suggests the Red Cross made a mistake when they thought Mr. Delalic was in charge. The Defence suggests the Bosnian army made mistakes in December of 1992 when they thought Mr. Delalic was in charge. The Defence suggests a number of Delalic's friends were lying when they said he was in charge in the seized material. The Defence suggests Mr. Mucic was mistaken or lying in 1992, during the camp's existence, when he told people that Mr. Delalic was in charge and making decisions. Defence suggests Mr. Mucic was lying when he wrote down later on that Mr. Delalic had been his superior. Defence suggests that Mr. Delalic was lying when he wrote down in a number of different documents, some of which had nothing to do with countering any propaganda campaign; they suggest Mr. Delalic was lying in all of it. And, of course, the Defence suggests that when Mr. Delalic signs orders which say "I order you to do this, and you are responsible to me for implementation of this order," it doesn't mean Mr. Delalic is actually ordering something; as Mr. Delalic said in his interview, "That's just a typing mistake." The Defence then also suggests that when Mr. Delalic's friends testify that he was not in charge of Celebici, these friends are now neither mistaken nor lying. And consider the Defence witnesses for a minute. I don't have time to discuss them individually, but I would like to as a group. The Defence witnesses would have you believe no one was in charge of Celebici, either de jure or de facto. The Defence witnesses all corroborated the evidence of the Prosecution, that there were no regulations on who should run prisons in 1992. The Defence witnesses agree it was a military prison and they agree that the MUP and the HVO withdrew early in the camp's existence. And the Defence witnesses agreed even though many of the guards were from the TO, the TO generally did not run the camp, in fact. So Defence suggests no one was in charge of the camp. It just existed for more than six months without anyone supervising it and without anyone having superior authority. The Prosecution submits this is incredible as a matter of common sense and further the Prosecution submits that this is contradicted by the evidence, the evidence shows someone was in charge in fact, and someone gave instructions to the persons who worked there and someone signed release documents for the prisoners, someone dealt with outside bodies, including media and international organisation, someone gave orders to the camp command and that someone was Mr. Delalic. I want to ask you specifically to consider one last thing when evaluating the credibility of the Defence witnesses and the weight to be given their testimony. These witnesses testified with great authority that Mr. Delalic did not have authority over Celebici. But they also said, when asked in cross-examination, that they did not know who was in charge of Celebici. These witnesses were also not in a position to know all of Mr. Delalic's responsibility or activities. So how could they say he didn't have any authority? Your Honours, the most these witnesses could have said is, credibly said, was that they didn't have any information that Mr. Delalic was a superior over the camp. But for a minute let's accept much of the Defence testimony, we'll accept Mr. Delalic's authority as coordinator and TO soldier and later as Tactical Group commander was not such that it would have normally encompassed Celebici camp. Let's accept the defence suggestion that is with respect to those instances where we see Mr. Delalic involved in the camp and even exercising authority, in all these different instances, that he was acting on behalf of others. So, when he gave instructions to the investigation commission, that was on behalf of the TO and the HVO and the war presidency, when he signed release documents, that was on behalf of the TO commander, and he gave interviews about Celebici, that was on behalf of unidentified authorities who couldn't be located. When he dealt with the Red Cross, that was on behalf of the supreme command and, of course, when he gave orders to the Celebici command, that was on behalf of the supreme command. If one accepts all this, all it does is show that Mr. Delalic's authority over Celebici was delegated to him by others. It shows that others share in the responsibility. It shows his authority may have arisen out of the needs of the situation rather than out of his inherent authority. But it still shows that he was a superior regarding the camp. Let's go further. Even if one accepts that Mr. Delalic was not delegated full authority over Celebici, he was not made the direct superior of Mr. Mucic and he could not himself have dismissed him or others under him. Even accepting these propositions, under the law he is still a superior. By his involvement in the running of the camp, by his authority and influence, he still had certain responsibilities and under well established law, he has liability as a superior. Others may share that responsibility, and it may well be that his ultimate sentence should reflect the limits of his authority and the shared nature of it, but that he has liability as an authority, we submit, is clear. Again, I'm not going to review the law in detail, but as seen in our written submissions, even persons lacking authority to control directly the conduct of forces can be liable under superior authority where other means of preventing the commission of offences exist, including by reporting to others or even by resigning. A number of cases submitted, cited on pages 196 to 200 of our brief, Mumenthey, Roechling, Muto, found superior authority in analogous situations, including where the authority was a civilian with no ability to fire the guards, but who was a definite integral and important figure in the whole concentration camp set up. Here, it cannot be doubted that Mr. Delalic was a part of the Celebici camp and he did nothing. Even just taking the things he did, he was involved in, although he was a person to direct the investigation commission, he did nothing to ensure that they were able to finish its work or to find out why they didn't finish their work. On two different occasions when he was approached concerning specific prisoners who were in danger of being murdered or dying, he became involved in getting three of them released, but he did nothing to find out about the 300 or more others who obviously were still in peril. When he was interviewed on Bosnian television refuting reports that conditions were bad in Celebici, he did nothing to ensure that the information he gave was accurate. When he ordered the TO commander and then Mucic to finally do a legitimate classification of the prisoners, he did nothing to ensure that the order was carried out and, in fact, the order was not carried out until January of the next year. And when Mr. Delalic received the reports of the Red Cross, including the first reports which, according to his own admission in his OTP interviews, specifically talked about Hazim Delic mistreating prisoners, he did nothing to investigate or to stop Mr. Delic from doing this in the future. When asked about this, he said, "I sent these reports to further instances, and I did not consider it very important for myself because I dealt with other things which were much more important." Now, it cannot be doubted that Mr. Delalic could have done any number of things, including making inquiries, conducting an investigation, giving additional instructions, writing a report and even resigning. But Mr. Delic did none of these things, he was involved, he was an integral part of the oversight of this camp, and he did nothing. When earlier today I asked, well, how could these things happen in Celebici for so long without anyone doing anything, it's because many persons, including Mr. Delic, Mr. Mucic, and Mr. Delalic did nothing. And given their positions, the law of superior authority says they had to do something. To adopt the Defence suggestions that persons such as these three accused were not superior authorities and thus were not obliged to do anything would be to set out international law to its state prior to the second World War, if not even before that. To adopt the Defence suggestions would be to render superior authority inapplicable to much of what happens in today's world. Among other things, it would render international humanitarian law impotent over situations with paramilitaries. It would render it impotent over situations where the structures of the armies are still evolving. It would render it impotent over a situation where there is shared control of subordinates, but that is not the state of the law today, nor should it be. Indeed, such an approach would only encourage persons to ensure that lines of authority were shared or undefined or unwritten so that no one could be charged with responsibility. In conclusion, Your Honours, the evidence is there, the law is there, and the responsibility is there. All four accused bare responsibility for the crimes in Celebici. The evidence has established their guilt beyond a reasonable doubt and we respectfully submit it is the duty of this Tribunal to convict each of them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are going to reply in the order of which the accused have been charged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you allowed us at the beginning of this trial, the Defence attorneys have decided upon the order in which they will be speaking before this Trial Chamber. And, in that sense, we would be using the time as rationally as possible and to present each of the aspects of the defence as best as possible. In that sense, Your Honours, we felt that we would hear the defence for Mr. Delic, Mr. Tom Moran first, after hearing Mr. Moran, the defence of Mr. Delalic would take the floor and then Mr. Mucic's Defence counsel, and we would wind up by the Defence counsel of Mr. Landzo if that is acceptable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's perfectly acceptable as long as it suits your presentation of your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge Karibi-Whyte, Judge Odio-Benito, Judge Jan, may it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First, with the help of the usher, last night I was trying to edit my speech down and I figured the easiest thing to do was just give the Trial Chamber a copy of my outline. I want to do this quickly and see if I can give you some time back. Just for the ushers knowledge, the top four copies are correctly paginated, the last ones, pages 24 and 25 are reversed. I apologise for that. The interpreters have been provided copies. There are extra ones if they want and ones there for the Prosecution also. Your Honour, I've been tagged by my colleagues to discuss the law with you. And, of course, I'm welcoming questions, I think those are clearly appropriate, and as you will see from my outline the first thing I would like to discuss with the Trial Chamber is the burden of proof. There seems to be some confusion in at least the Prosecutor's written submission in that the Defence presented no evidence on something, there is no contention, that this is not true. It's my opinion, and I think it's the law, that the Prosecutor has the burden of proving all elements of each offence, beyond a reasonable doubt. That we have absolutely no obligation to do anything, that the Defence lawyers could have sat here, not said a word this entire trial and the presumption of innocence should be sufficient to convict us -- or excuse me, to acquit us. I'm sorry, Judge, it's been a long day. I was up until 3.00 this morning. I apologise. Mrs. McHenry said something that struck me, and I am just going to quote it out of my notes: "When it this is done and when the persons prove to be responsible for violations of the law are convicted, justice will have been achieved." Your Honours, justice is achieved when justice is an achieved. No Prosecutor has ever lost a case, their job is to see that justice is done. If there are a acquittals on all defendants on all counts, the Prosecutor has won the case, because they did not prove it beyond a reasonable doubt and justice has been done. Justice and convictions are two different things. Beyond a reasonable doubt, I have prepared a chart. Actually, with the help of the usher, this is a chart that I've used before to remind people about what is beyond a reasonable doubt. And it simply shows the various levels of evidence. And what it take to get to a guilty. And it starts off with no evidence at all. And it goes to a scintillae of evidence, just the tiniest bit of evidence, and that's a not guilty, or reasonable suspicion, where there are specific facts, that's a not guilty. It goes all the way up to clear and convincing evidence that it's a firm belief that the allegations are true And, under our system, that still is a not guilty. To get to a guilty, you have to go to the very top step on that chart, and that's proof that is so convincing that you would rely on it without hesitation in the most important of your own affairs. That's typical form in the United States as you've seen in my written submission. I understand in Britain the definition is: Are you sure? And you have to ask yourself when you retire to deliberate: Are you sure? In the High Command case, the trial court said when there is ambiguity in testimony or uncertainty as the defendant's connection as the transactions to rely upon to establish guilt, we have followed the well-recognised principle of common law and have accorded to the defendants the benefit of the doubt. That, I believe, is what any court should do. When there is a doubt, when there are ambiguities, it goes to the defendant. Credibility of witnesses. One of the toughest jobs any fact-finder has is judging witness credibility. I am an advocate. They're advocates. We see things through our set of glasses. And, as judges, it's your job to look at things neutrally and detached. To judge that credibility. I have suggested in my written submissions, a few things that I think may help you judge credibility of witnesses. The Prosecutor says the procedures here are foreign and intimidating to some of these witnesses. Well, except for professional witnesses, procedures in every court are foreign and intimidating to every witness, every citizen who witnesses a robbery or is involved in a traffic accident, has to come down to the court house to testify. Language problems. That's something that cuts both ways. Everyone has the same language problem. You've heard probably a hundred times in this trial, there is an interpretation problem. When you go back, I want you to recall, there is a book out about the title of which is, "Truth is the first casualty in a war." We're talking about a trial that arose during a war. And not only that, but we're talking about a situation where people who were involved in that war are still in power in various countries. They have power in Bosnia-Herzegovina there and power in Croatia there and power in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Each one of them, each one of those parties has its interests and it has its people and there may be hidden agendas out there. And I think you should look at that. Prior statements. I think you can look at a witness' prior statement to see if it's consistent. To see how it flows with what he said on that witness stand. Evasiveness. I cited Judge Karibi-Whyte in my written submission where there was somebody who just didn't want to answer a question and Judge Karibi-Whyte said, this is becoming common in this trial or words to that effect. I have got the exact cite there. All of those things show whether or not a witness is telling the truth. Then you have on at least a couple of occasions, direct contradictions between Prosecution witnesses. The best example, and it's one that I have cited and one that I am relying upon is between Grozdana Cecez and Witness T. The Prosecution brought both of these witnesses to you. And they said these are witnesses for the truth. We're bringing them here because they're going to be witnesses for the truth. And what happened? Ms. Cecez said Witness T raped me. And Witness T said it's a made up story. Who are you to believe? Another incident of direct contradiction involved two of the Prosecution expert witnesses: Professor Economides and Professor Gow, related to the end of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. On re-examination, Mr. Niemann brought out that from Professor Economides that the SFRY didn't end until April -- or, excuse me, until September 1992. Why was that? So it would show dual citizenship. What does Professor Gow say? No. The latest possible date was April 27th, 1992. Why is that important? Again, it shows direct contradictions between the Prosecutor's witnesses. People they brought you as witnesses for the truth. Prisoner of war status. I frankly find this rather incredible. I have cited in my written submission several cases, I think seven or eight. Where if you are to believe that these people or any of them were prisoners of war under the conventions, you have to believe, and the Prosecutor has to convince you, that their own witnesses are not credible. That has to be the Prosecutor's position. Because those people testified in such a way that they could not be prisoners of war. I find this just -- something I have never seen before. Where they're making a legal argument which is based on the incredibility of their own witnesses. Incredible stories. If a witness tells an incredible story, you shouldn't believe him. How about Risto Vukalo? He sat in that chair right over there and he told you that a statement from him to the Office of the Prosecutor was coerced because of the guards. That he was afraid that the same thing was going to happen to him that happened in Celebici. And he would have said milk was black. I don't believe that their investigators had great big hulking guards there to threaten people to get witness statements. Bronco Sudar, the man who testified about the ghastly things that happened to him in the Celebici camp. And then you found out he could have left, but decided to stay. That ought to be very, very helpful in judging his credibility. I suggest to you there are two witnesses who are very credible: One of theirs and one of mine. They're credible because they're neutral. Esad Harraz, the Egyptian journalist. They called and put on the stand as a witness for the truth. He is the only person who testified in this trial who was in the camp at the applicable times and is neutral, who does not have an axe to grind. What did he tell you about those conditions in that camp? He didn't see any prisoners that were beaten. He didn't see any evidence of starvation. He didn't see any mistreatment and he didn't take part in any mistreatment. Medical supplies in Building 22 appeared to be about right for the number of patients. Now, that, one, goes to the fact of the case. There is something else that goes to credibility of witnesses. Because several witnesses, Witness M, Miro Golubovic, Novica Dordic, Risto Vukalo and Witness J and Witness R, sat on that witness stand and told you that the Arab television crew either filmed beatings or participated in them. Another witness, I think is the witness for the truth is Eduardo Bellas. Dr. Bellas was brought here to talk about the scientific evidence. If the Prosecution witnesses had been telling the truth, if their testimony was factual, what in all likelihood would have been the scientific results of that kind of treatment? And what did he tell you? There would have been infectious diseases. You don't have to be a PhD in epidemiology to figure out that if people are eating food with faeces on it, drinking water with pieces of faeces in it, that you're going to have infectious diseases. You didn't hear any testimony about massive outbreaks of infectious disease. Heat stroke. The kinds of temperatures, the water, lack of water that the Prosecution witnesses testified about. A litre and three or four people have to share it. You would have had dead people from heat exhaustion. Where are they? You didn't hear about them. Esad Landzo, special case. The Prosecutor can't decide whether Esad Landzo is a truth teller or he is not a truth teller. Part of the time in their written submission, they say he is a liar. And part of the time they rely on him, his testimony for the truth of the matter. I suggest as to Esad Landzo's testimony, the Prosecutor ought to pick a horse and ride it. He is either a truth teller or he is not and you know my position. Let's talk about the statute of the Tribunal for a second. The actual statute itself and what it is and what it does. There seems to be some confusion, at least on the Prosecution side and maybe on my side as to what the statute of the Tribunal is. In my view, and I think the view of the Secretary-General and security counsel. The statute of the Tribunal does not create crimes, does not define crimes. Does not create any substance of offences. If it did, my client is not guilty because the statute was not passed until about six months or seven months after the last offence alleged in the indictment. What the statute of the Tribunal does is it sets up a court. It sets up a Tribunal to hear allegations of some types of violations of pre-existing international law. Statute doesn't create law. The knew Rome statute does. The statute that was passed in Rome last month, creates law. It creates offences, defines offences. It does that because it's a treaty process which most of the nations of the world, most of the civilised nations have agreed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is quite right. He comes from the United States, that is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, some day we'll talk about Jesse Helms. The security counsel is not a legislative body -- or, for that matter, the general assembly does not have the authority to do this on its own, to define legislation. Another area is this: The Prosecutor has failed to prove, failed to present any proof that the Geneva Conventions and their protocols or their protocols were, in effect, and applicable to these defendants. I know that sounds crazy, but that, in fact, is the truth. And Professor Bassiouni says that Bosnia-Herzegovina acceded to the conventions on December 31st, 1992. They were not applicable as conventional, international law. International armed conflict. We beat this thing to death. Just one thing I would point out to the Trial Chamber and then I'll move on to something else. In Paragraph 6.83 of the Prosecutor's submission they talk about a May 22nd, 1992, agreement under common Article 3 of the conventions. What they're saying is that the parties expected the grave breaches, clauses and provisions of the conventions to apply. Well, if you take a look at what the Prosecutor says in that paragraph, it says that the parties to the conflict were the government of the Republic of Herzegovina, the SDA party, SDS party, the Serb party and the Croatian party. Nowhere in that agreement on May 22nd, 1992, do you see anybody except Bosnians. That's their argument. They're not happy with the Appeals Chamber ruling and the Trial Chamber ruling in the Tadic case. It's the law. I would suggest also that the member for commission on experts did say that after May 1992, when the JNA was ordered to split and all those events occurred, it became an internal armed conflict at the times applicable to this case. It's cited in my written submission, Commander Fenrick, who I believe the Prosecutors are familiar with, to his government, the Canadian government, suggested that prior to April 6th, 1992, when Bosnia became an independent state, it was an internal armed conflict. April 6th through May 19th, international armed conflict became internal armed conflict again on the 19th of May. Why is this important? Well, obviously it's important to their argument. It's something else. It's important for another reason. This Court is not a court of general jurisdiction. This is a court of limited jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why don't you say special jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the phrase we would use in my country is limited. I think, probably, special better. This Trial Chamber does not have the right to, for instance, hear a case for a genocide in Rwanda. The Prosecutor as the plaintiff, bears the burden of showing, proving, that this Trial Chamber, this Tribunal has jurisdiction. They made a jurisdictional allegation in their indictment, international armed conflict. I would submit to you that if they don't prove international armed conflict, they have failed to prove that this Tribunal has subject matter jurisdiction. Why else is it important? Obviously for the Article 2 counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually is that what Article 1 gives the courts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Article 1 sets out the Tribunal's jurisdiction. But international armed conflict is also important for the Article 2 counts in the indictment. The Prosecutor said that we would have that read narrowly. You bet we would. We would have the words of the Geneva Convention be interpreted to mean what they say on paper. That the plain language of the Statute be interpreted or be applied. We say that when the Geneva convention on civilians says, in the hands of a party of which they are not nationals, that's what it means. It doesn't mean identification with a different side or anything else. It means what the parties to the convention agree to. Nothing more, nothing less. In a hostages case, another thing that the Court there said is that criminal laws are to be interpreted narrowly. That that is the way that criminal law should be interpreted. We're asking you to interpret it like it's written and if that's narrow and if the Prosecutor isn't happy about that, then maybe the Prosecutor ought to be in Geneva talking to the Red Cross about having the Geneva Conventions of 2001 and to change them. You should interpret the laws as they're written. Common Article 3. The Trial Chamber is well aware, it's my position, it was Mr. Ackerman's position when he was here, it was everyone's position that at least prior to the adoption of the Rwanda statute there was no indication that common Article 3 provided for individual criminal liability. I think that the new Rome statute makes that even clearer. That when it lists crimes, the Rome statute does two things with common Article 3; one, it talks about laws and customs of war, and then it goes on to talk about common Article 3. The second thing that the Rome statute does is recognise the common Article 3 applies for individual criminal liability only in internal armed conflicts. Just like it says in the conventions. The Prosecutor would give a very, very broad reading. I'll admit that under the Tadic appeals' decision, it's clearly a legitimate reading. In fact, it's probably consistent with what the Tadic court said. I would just assert that it is wrongly decided. Now, I think you're bound by it. But I think I also have to raise the issue here in order to ask the Appeals Chamber to reconsider in Tadic. I would suggest to you that there is no proof that's been presented to this Trial Chamber, or, for that matter in the Tadic case, that the nations of the world have adopted as customary, international law, individual criminal liability for violations of common Article 3. The one case, and I am scared to cite this case -- because I am probably talking to its author -- the one case that the Appeals Chamber cited from that proposition was from the Nigeria Supreme Court, a 1972 case. I pulled the case and read it. It appeared to me that the defendant in that case was charged under Nigerian law with murder. That the Supreme Court simply mentioned in passing that international law doesn't allow you to murder people during conflicts. Even if common Article 3 provides for individual criminal liability, there has to be some evidence before the Trial Chamber, if it's customary international law, who is protected? Who do the nations of the world believe that international law requires them to protect under common Article 3 as customary international law during an international armed conflict? There is zero evidence of that. The Prosecutor bears the burden of showing you that factor. I would suggest that common Article 3 as applied to international armed conflict provides most people with very little protection and, in fact, does not provide any protection to most people. It's clear that the authors of the convention chose not to interfere with the right of a nation, at least in an international armed conflict to deal with its own nationals. That's why the definition in Article 4 of the convention on civilians is written the way it is. In fact, dictator's commentary says that. "The convention remains faithful to the recognised principle of international. It does not interfere in a states' relations with its own nationals." When you think about it, it really is pretty logical. In an internal armed conflict, which is what common Article 3 was designed and written to regulate, the presumption that a government protects its own people falls. The government is fighting with its own people. So there has to be some international law protection there. When governments engage in crimes against humanity and genocide, there is international law protection there to protect people from their own governments. To protect the Jews from the Nazis. But, generally, it is not the business of international law on how the United States government treats me or the Australian treats Mr. Niemann. That is between us and our government, so long as they don't engage in genocide and crimes against humanity. I would suggest that the class of people who are protected by common Article 3 in an international armed conflict are very narrow indeed. That would include such things as nationals of neutral states that have diplomatic relations with the parties. Or possibly nationals of states who are not bound by the Geneva Convention on civilians, therefore, depriving their own nationals of protection when they're in other countries. Protected persons. The Prosecutor has to prove two things: One, they have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt there is international armed conflict. The second thing that the Prosecutor has to do as a matter of law is show that the individual named as a complainant in that indictment was a protected person under the conventions. The Prosecutor seems to try and mull this, that you don't have to decide the nationality of each person. They've said that and they've said that and they've said that. The fact that those people are protected or not protected is an element of the Prosecutor's offence. They're trying to shift the burden of proof to us. They're trying to avoid having to prove the elements of their case and meet their burden of proof. They want to ignore the plain wording of the convention. There is no evidence before this Trial Chamber. None. Zero. That the people who were named in that indictment were not nationals of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. None. The Prosecutor says the evidence led by the Defence on the actual citizenship of detainees is relevant and is not required to show that they were not non-nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's contrary to what Dr. Economides told you, their expert. That's contrary to law. They know it is. They bear the burden of proving non-nationality. If you look at paragraph 2 of the indictment, the Prosecutor says: Beginning in the later part of May, 1992, forces consisting of Bosnian Muslims -- it's on page 9 of my outline Your Honour -- and Bosnian Croats attacked and took control of those villages containing predominantly Bosnian Serbs. Why do we call them Bosnian Serbs? Why does the Prosecutor call them Bosnian Serbs? Because they're Bosnians. That's why. That is not only a judicial admission, that is their assertion. They are asserting to you that they are Bosnian Serbs. Bosnians. Paragraph 76 of the Tadic appellate decision. When you look at paragraph 76 of the court's appellate it has a hypothetical. That decision was handed down about five or six months before the Celebici indictment was returned. And, lo and behold, the hypothetical used by the Appeals Chamber is Celebici. Bosnian Serbs in the hands of the Bosnian government. And what does the Appeals Chamber say in the hypothetical? Not an Article 2 violation because they are not in the hands of a party of which they were not nationals. The Prosecutor doesn't like it, doesn't have to like it. That's what the Appeals Chamber says, that's what the law is. This identified with a nationality, shouldn't be considered nationals argument, it doesn't have any foundation in the law. It's a request to ignore the plain wording of Article 4 of the Geneva Convention on civilians it's a request for you to ignore Pictet's commentaries. They say the conventions don't have a definition of nationality. Of course it doesn't. Nationality is a term of art in international law. It has a meaning, we all know what that meaning is. It has a specific meaning, Dr. Economides told you what it is. Then they try to confuse, I think, confuse the issue by citing the Belsen case. The Belsen case involved Polish nationals who were charged with and convicted of war crimes against nationals of other allied powers in the Bergen Belsen concentration camp. And the Prosecution takes the position this shows you can be convicted of war crimes against people who are on the same side of a war that you're on or the same nationality you are. Sure it does. But it ignores, fails to mention the factor in the hands of a party to the conflict of which they were not nationals. The Bergen Belsen concentration camp was a German camp, and the Poles and the French and the English and the Americans in that camp were in the hands of a party to the conflict of which they were not nationals. Germany. They were in the hands of the other side. It was a German camp run by the Germans. The Prosecutor makes, in paragraph 6.93 makes a policy argument that if you're going to hold Bosnian Serbs guilty of grave breaches against Bosnian Muslims, presuming the Prosecutor can ever get around to proving an international armed conflict, then it ought to work the other way around. The Prosecution's position in the Tadic case, and I agree with their proposition of law, I just disagree with their factual analysis. But their proposition of law was that the Republic of Srpska and its army were controlled by the agents of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. If that is true, then the Bosnian Muslims who were in Omarska and the other places were in the hands of a party of which they were not nationals, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Paragraph 76 of Tadic, since it cannot be contended that the Bosnian Serbs constitute a state. Clear. Secondly, our position is consistent with the nationality position, citizenship position taken in the Dayton Accords. Article 7A of the Bosnian constitution, the Dayton Accords, says all citizens of either the Republic of Srpska or the Federation are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. 7C says that everybody who was a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina immediately before the date of the Dayton Accords are citizens of BH, and it provides for dual nationality. The entire purpose of the Dayton Accords was to arrive at peace by having one country. This Tribunal is a creature of the Security Council to do what; bring about the restoration of peace in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It would be ironic as anything if this Tribunal were to make a decision on a matter of law which is contrary to the Dayton Accords which is the agreement to bring about peace. Those people in the Celebici camp were Bosnian nationals, or even if they weren't, the Prosecutor has not proved they were not. Identification with either side does not make any difference. Finally, on this issue, if you take their argument about people being associated with one side or another, really what you're doing is you're having a charter of rights for aggressors. Adolf Hitler in 1938 could have said the people in the Sudetenland are Germans, they're identified with Germany, and I'm going to send the Wehrmacht in to help my Germans, to protect my Germans. Slobodan Milosevic could take their argument and say those Bosnian Serbs are identified with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I have to send the tanks into Bosnia-Herzegovina to protect my people. Identification with one side, ethnicity, no difference. Nationality. Prisoners of war. As I mentioned earlier, I find this argument amazing. Article 4 of the Geneva Convention, on prisoners of war, defines who is a prisoner of war. One of the things they have to show, Article 4 paragraph 2 of the Geneva Conventions on prisoners of war, page 13 of my outline; if they are a partisan movement, they have to belong to a party to the conflict. Which party to the conflict did the Prosecutor prove beyond a reasonable doubt these people belonged to? Which one? I haven't heard. There's no showing that these people were in anybody's regular army. There's no showing of a chain of command with a commander responsible for his subordinates. Testimony of the Prosecutor's witness negates prisoner of war status, I lay it out in my written submission. Levee en masse: A levee en masse is where people rise up spontaneously to stop the invader. How can Bosnia-Herzegovina invade Bosnia-Herzegovina? That's right out of the Wizard of Oz. International humanitarian law tries to split people into two groups, basically; combatants and non-combatants, when it comes to how wars are waged. And combatants are legitimate targets. When I wore a green suit and I was carrying an M-16, I was a legitimate target. And that guy wearing a different uniform and carrying an AK-47 was a legitimate target. And you try to keep those groups separated from people who are non-combatants. And to the extent possible, international humanitarian law requires that non-combatants be protected. If you look at the Hostages case, it talks about legitimate combatants and illegitimate combatants. And if you do not come under the definition of a combatant in Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions, and presuming the protocols apply under Protocol I, you do not have the right to engage in combat. The Prosecutor is trying to blur this distinction. And when you blur this distinction, what are you going to have? You're going to have legitimate combatants who are worried about being shot in the back, they are going to shoot first and ask questions later. You cannot let the line between legitimate combatants and non-combatants be blurred. Command responsibility. Prosecutor accuses me of giving an incredibly narrow reading to the Article 2, the types of offences that can be charged under Article 2. They have given an incredibly broad meaning to the word superior, I mean, just incredibly. Everybody is a superior. There seems to be some confusion over what a chain of command is. In their submission, their written submission, they talk about a chain of command in a way that I believe is inappropriate. A chain of command -- well, command responsibility began as the liability of a military commander to control his troops. And it says that he is liable under international law if he fails to carry out his duty to prevent his people from committing war crimes. That's all command responsibility is about. It's nothing magic. That's that duty on that commander. Now, since World War II, in fact in some of the post World War II cases, Tokyo and others, there was a look at command responsibility for non-military commanders. Commander Fenrick and most of the commentators seem to agree that that kind of authority has to be a military command-like authority. This is different from rank in the military. Command is the right by virtue of a person's office and a special assignment to command a military unit. Only that commander has the right to issue orders in his own name and enforce it. The Hostages case, high command case all talk about that. Rank is something different. Rank is where you sit on the degree of precedence within the military; but clearly, non commanders are in units where they have greater rank than commanders. The Toyoda case, which the Prosecutor cites, is an example of that. Admiral Toyoda was the highest ranking admiral in the Japanese navy, and he was charged in the atrocities committed by Japanese naval forces in Manila that General Matsui was hanged for. And he was found not guilty. Why? Not because he didn't have more rank than those Japanese naval forces. He had more rank than any other Japanese naval officer. He was found not guilty because he was not the commander, General Yamashida was the commander. There is a lot of factors in command responsibility, but the two I would point to quickly are the nature and the extent of authority. The nature of authority to be held criminally liable, a military commander or superior, whatever you want to call him, has to be able to, one, issue legally binding orders; and two, he has to be able to enforce those orders with criminal sanctions. That's the distinction between a military commander and the civilian superior with military command-like authority and every other boss in the world. My boss at home can fire me, he can tell me get out of the office, never come back, but he can't send me to gaol. It's not going to be very common you're going to find a non commander superior that is going to have this kind of authority. I suspect that most of the time it's going to be a very, very high ranking person, almost a cabinet level officer. One example cited by the Prosecutor is the Pohl case, cited under paragraph 4.127 of their submission. In that case the Court said Pohl was either a commander or he had the same kind of power as a commander. That, I believe is the correct test. And you have to look at the extent of his authority. So, you have to be able to see what kind of power he has, how he can enforce that power. And then the Prosecutor still gets to prove that he didn't do it. You can't just say there were crimes, this guy is a commander, the crimes didn't stop, or this guy is a superior, the crimes didn't stop, he's guilty. That's the kind of absolute responsibility, absolute liability that the Yamashida case is criticised for and that nobody says exists. Take a look at Article 25 of the Rome Statute. That lays out what I believe is the most recent example of how the nations of the world view customary international law as it applies to command/superior responsibility. And another thing to look at in my written submission is the proposed Article 25, with a footnote, footnote 11 of that report. And what that footnote says is everybody wanted to broaden this beyond military command-like authority; so that's why this draft article is written this way. But if you look at the finally adopted article, it's a lot different from the draft article. It shows the intent of the nations of the world and what they believe is customary law. Extent of authority. Prosecutor's submission, paragraph 4.124; no one can be identified as having been entrusted with specific formal authority over the camp commander or the camp. Nor can the formal limits of Delalic's authority as coordinator or commander of TG-1 be identified with any great precision. They have got to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Zejnil Delalic had the authority to do these things, and they tell you in writing they don't know what the extent of his authority is. It's Oz. Mucic, no surprise to the Trial Chamber, you handed down a decision about two weeks ago, you said there is no oral or written evidence as to the extent of Mucic's authority or the nature of it. It's not even clear from the record whether Mucic is a military commander or whether Mucic is a civilian prison warden. They just haven't proved it. The record is clear that there's a whole bunch of groups running all over the Celebici camp; there's TIO, HVO, MUP. Their Witness T testified that people would come running in, in the night, and be doing horrible things to prisoners and the guards couldn't stop them. Their Witness T said he was afraid of them. One thing is sure, though; no matter how much authority and what kind of authority Pavo Mucic had in that camp, Hazim Delic had to have the same or less. He couldn't have any more if he was Pavo's deputy. Knowledge. Another thing they have to prove is knowledge. A whole lot of different formulations floating around. The Rome Statute adopts a knew or should have known standard. The indictment uses a lower standard, knew or had reason to know. Protocol I has two different versions. One version says the commander had to have possessed information which should have enabled them to conclude, should. The French version, in English says, possessed information enabling them to conclude. The Prosecutor has to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that this kind of information was out there to Hazim Delic, Pavo Mucic, Zejnil Delalic, and I would suggest that given the fact that criminal laws should be interpreted narrowly, given the fact that Commander Fenrick has written this French version should be used because it is narrower, the Prosecution's feet should be held to the fire and they should be required to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that people they are charging in a command responsibility theory possessed information enabling them to conclude there were war crimes going on. Let me digress for a second and talk about my client individually. There's no evidence he was a commander at any applicable time in this trial. At most he was a deputy at some point. It's not clear exactly what day he began being deputy and what day he stopped. As I've said, the evidence is real murky, unclear. Failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt what authority Pavo Mucic had. By failing to show what Pavo, what authority Pavo had, and what the nature of his authority was, because Mr. Delic cannot have more authority than his boss, they failed to prove what Hazim had, what authority and what the nature of that authority was. The Prosecutor says he could have done this or that. In fact, there was a commander of the guard, there's plenty of testimony about that, there was testimony from Esad Landzo that Mr. Mucic appointed somebody as commander of the guard. That person was not Hazim Delic. Chain of command in the camp from one commander to another, if it's a military unit it goes from camp commander to the commander of the guard, leaves out the deputy. The leading cases, and I've beaten them to death, are List and von Leeb. The Prosecutor relies on the Muto decision out of the Tokyo Tribunal to show that a deputy commander can be held responsible on the command responsibility theory. What they forgot to do was give you the full quotation. On page 20 of my outline I've given you the other paragraphs there. It seems to indicate, at least my reading, at one time he was a commander, and at another time he was a staff officer, and then he was a deputy commander; and the Japanese troops were engaged in all kinds of ghastly things there. It's not clear from the judgement whether he was convicted for his time as a commander. You look at the authorities that the Prosecution cites in its written submission as it applies to Hazim Delic, and every one of them, on the paper that they sent you, talks about commanders. They look at ICRC commentaries to Protocol I, talks about commanders. You look at the citations from von Leeb and Colonel John Douglas, who was the former commander of the US Army Judge Advocate General school, talks about the criminal liability of non commanders for their own acts. Not for the acts of others. Mens rea for homicide. The statute and the conventions -- I'm informed Mr. Greaves is going to talk about that, so I will skip on to something else. I was not going to discuss individual counts of the indictment, but there are two counts, or two groups of counts that apply specifically to Mr. Delic, and that's the two rape counts. I've laid it out in my written submission why I think there is a reasonable doubt there, but I will suggest a couple of factors to the Trial Chamber. One, neither one of them could pick him out of a photo spread. It's in evidence, the photo array is in evidence. Delic exhibit 1.
