On judging Mrs. Cecez's credibility, I've seen evasive on cross and I've seen evasive on cross, and then I've seen Mrs. Cecez's; she sat on that witness stand and told you that she didn't remember whether she made corrections in her prior written statements the day before she sat on that witness stand. She sat on that witness stand and told you she didn't remember whether she was interviewed on television. I'm not going to say whether that is true or not. I'm going to suggest one or two things as a possibility: Either she remembered and didn't want to say so, which goes to her credibility; or in the alternative, she didn't remember, she was telling you the truth from the witness stand. And if that's true, how can she recall events from five years before? If she can't remember what she did yesterday and recount it to you, it goes directly to her ability to recall and recount events accurately. Mrs. Antic. Prosecutor beats me up pretty good in their written submission for my cross-examination of Mrs. Antic. And I wasn't trying to embarrass her, I was trying to get some specific information. And if there's any embarrassment there, I apologise to the Court. Judge Jan and Judge Karibi-Whyte and I talked to her about the hysterectomy and birth control pills. The direct quote is in my written submission. I think Judge Jan said it is a big operation, and every woman knows that, and Judge Karibi-Whyte said it's not getting a wart removed, I think. utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to start by putting to you a proposition, which I hope is not controversial in any way. But one which is a matter of common sense. It's this: That any system of criminal law, whether that be a national municipal system of criminal law or a system of international criminal law, requires -- demands, that it laws be clear, precise and formulated in readily accessible language. It doesn't always happen, sadly. As anyone who has an had an opportunity to see the English court of appeal engage in some act of semantic dishonesty. But as a proposition, it is a good one in my submission. The purpose of that proposition is this: That the laws may be clearly understood by those to whom the laws apply, be they citizen, states or armies. That implementation of the criminal law does not fail because the laws lack clarity, precision and readily acceptable language. Allowing the guilty to evade justice, or worse, causing the innocent to be unjustly convicted. Thirdly, that those charged with trying and sentencing criminals can do so in the knowledge that the system they are applying, enjoys the confidence of the people. Fourthly, and perhaps as important as any of those, that those whose task it is to advise others on the law, can give clear and ambiguous and proper advice, whether that be to prosecutors or to defendants. The reasons why that proposition is important is because in the criminal courts, in every jurisdiction, there is the power to send people to prison for the rest of their life. In some jurisdictions, there is the power to deprive people of their life. Those are fundamental acts that involve the liberty and life of the subject. For that reason, all systems of criminal law must meet the criteria that I have suggested. If we look at the Geneva Conventions, we find that those are not criminal statutes. The intention in 1949 and reinforced in 1977, is that national jurisdictions should implement the philosophy of the Geneva Conventions by passing into their own legislation, suitable and appropriate acts of parliament, designed to meet their own legal system. An example in my jurisdiction, in England and Wales, is the Genocide Act of 1969, which imports into English law, the Geneva Conventions grave breaches scheme and makes it part of our criminal law. The consequences of having as the background to war crimes trials at the Geneva Conventions, is that we as the source from which the statute of the Tribunal is derived, a series of documents which are not intended to be criminal statutes. They don't begin, in my submission, to match the status of what most jurisdictions would recognise as criminal statutes or criminal codes. What we do have is the statute of the Tribunal. I move on now to this point: When it comes to the question of interpretation of that statute and what definitions you should give in our submission to the meanings of words, phrases and language, we urge Your Honours to continue to do as you have done throughout this trial. To interpret language by applying the ordinary and usual meaning to the words, phrases and language that you have to define. We urge you to continue to do that because that is a fair and proper way of dealing with interpretation. I turn now to the bulk of what I have to say. Firstly, I deal with the question of mens rea of murder. At the conclusion of the Prosecution case, we set out a reasonably basis for a proper means of construing the offence of murder. It is a matter of regret that, thus far, the Prosecution have largely failed to address the serious issues that were raised in that submission. By and large what they say is, well, we're right, the Defence are wrong and we don't need to argue the point. In their submissions, they rely entirely on the ICRC commentary to Protocol 1. That, in itself, contains language that is incorrect we submit and we remind you of it. Wilfully, the accused must have acted consciously and with intent i.e., with his mind on the act and its consequences and willing the result, criminal intent or malice of forethought, which is actually an incorrect use of English. It's malice of aforethought, one word. And it then goes in to import into the definition, the concept of recklessness. The problem, we submit, for the Prosecution, lies in the words actually used in the statute. It is those words that Your Honours have to construe. In the English version of the Statute, it is wilful killing. In the French version it is Homicide Intentional. Now, rightly we don't look to national law to define the words and phrases that are part of the criminal law of this Tribunal. Your Honours may think that the definition that in their various submissions that they have made, that the Prosecution have essentially latched on to the classic English definition of the law of murder. Well, they then proceed to muddle it by adding the concept of recklessness. Your Honours, the definition in England is that you can be guilty of murder if you intend to kill or intend to do really serious bodily harm. But it doesn't have as part of its definition, recklessness. But they seem to echo in the phrase that they use, the English definition, which I am sure it may well be that definition still exists in other commonwealth jurisdictions and Your Honours will be more familiar with your own than I. I said a moment ago that Your Honours should approach these kinds of words by using the ordinary and usual meanings of them. That, in my submission, is the starting point from which you should proceed. In the submissions we made at the conclusion of the Prosecution case, we quoted from respectable dictionaries. They clearly point to what the ordinary and usual meaning of the words in the statute in English and French are. Intentional qui est fait expres, avec intention, a dessein. Conscient, delibere, premedite, volontaire, voulu... And perhaps importantly, in connection with the law, droit, Delit intentional, par opposé au delit d'imprudence et au delit contraventionnel. As opposed to a crime of imprudence or negligence or recklessness. We say that that is a clear indication of what the word "intentional" was intended to mean in the legislation. The Oxford English -- that comes from La Grande Française, 1989. The word "wilful," the Oxford English dictionary, the large version thereof. Done on purpose or wittingly, purpose, deliberate, intentional and not accidental or casual. We submit that it is quite clear what those words mean. They are clear and unambiguous definitions. In English and in French. Of course, and I speak only of my own language, to say that intention and recklessness can be the same thing is simply to stand the English language on its head. They are two concepts which both in law and in common sense are mutually exclusive. We say that construing the statute in the manner that I have invited Your Honours to do so can lead to only one conclusion. That the proper definition of wilful murder Homicide intentional is killing with the intent to kill. I turn now to torture. The Prosecution demonstrated in their submissions, the inconsistency of their approach. Because in respect of torture, having said that the ICRC was the definitive law for murder, the ICRC commentaries, when it suits them they ignore the ICRC commentary. On this occasion the ICRC commentary doesn't suit, so they have to go and look for another source. On this occasion, it was the 1984 convention which gave them the lead to define what they say torture is. They also quote extensively from Sherry Bassiouni's book. Again, unfortunately, it's somewhat selective because there is another proposition which is put by Mr. Bassiouni at page 549 of his book concerning the definition of torture. Your Honours will forgive me for reading it, but it's important. Additionally Section F of Article 6. Torture is criminalised by the Torture Convention. That's the 1984 convention. But the Torture Convention is not included in the statutes listed applicable substantive law. Furthermore, that the acts enumerated in this provision are undefined and the elements of the offences are unstated, raises questions concerning the principles of legality. How the Tribunal should determine the definition and elements of the prohibited acts is left unresolved. The Tribunal could rely on the definition and elements of the corresponding crimes contained in the criminal codes of the previous republics in which the alleged acts occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are being implored to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I heard and didn't want to lose the thread of what I was saying. This approach would ensure that the substantive aspects of the principles of legality are upheld. It would be consistent also with Article 22 which provides that the Tribunal should impose penalties after considering the laws of the various republics. Alternatively, the tribunal could disregard applicability of domestic law and rely on general principles of law to ascertain the elements of such crimes in the world's major criminal justice systems. This approach, however, would require a substantial comparative criminal law research project. The Tribunal does not have the resources, personnel or time for such an undertaking. Torture and rape are included within the meaning other inhuman acts of Article 6(c) of the IMT Charter. However, the Tribunal must still identify the legal elements of those crimes. As previously indicated, the Tribunal could rely on the applicable criminal laws of the former republics. BiH, Croatia and Serbia has similar substantive criminal laws. The tribunal, therefore, would interpret the stature in a matter that is consistent in substance with the principles of legality. The report of the Secretary-General does not mention the torture convention, which nevertheless should provide the definition for torture under F. So it's his submission, effectively, that the 1984 convention is the appropriate one. But his opinion falls short, we submit, of being settled law. There is support for that. Firstly, Article 1 of the 1984 convention speaks of the definition given there being for the purposes of this convention. It may be that that is a restrictive clause. Secondly, that definition of torture is not unique. There are other definitions given in other jurisdictions. In the case of Ireland versus the United Kingdom, in 1978, before the European Court of Human Rights, that court had to deal with a complaint by the Irish government that the British were torturing Irish terrorists. The conduct complained of was forcing people to stand against walls for long periods of time by their finger tips, causing them to become disorientated, by hooding suspects, again with the intention of disorientating, by subjecting them to white noise pending interrogations, by depriving them of sleep and by depriving them of food and drink. The Court held that that was not torture. I draw that decision to Your Honour's attention. I won't go through it in detail because of the time aspect, but I draw it to your attention. It is important. It contains another definition of torture. Next, in 1985, the year after the 1984 convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just before you proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There is. I am not going to read it out because it's a lengthy passage and I am constrained by time. I draw the decision to Your Honours' decision and you can draw upon it leisure and I urge it upon you. Is that helpful?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you say it is not torture, then there must be some definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: They do indeed define what torture is as far as they concerned, but they say that those acts, cumulatively, did not amount to torture. And our submission would be that the acts that were being carried on involving Irish terrorists were far more serious and grave and perhaps the classic thing that people and plainly the Irish government thought of it as torture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I don't understand that. White noise?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, when your ear phones play a mushy sounding noise, that is known as white noise and that was the noise that was played to them. And if it's played to you for long periods of time, it's very disorientating, just ask any 15-year-old that goes to the disco. And Judge Odio-Benito would possibly know more about the 1985 Inter-American Convention to prevent and punish torture. That was signed in Colombia in 1985 and that has yet another definition of torture which is similar to, but is certainly not identical with the definition proposed by the Prosecution. And I see her acknowledging that that exists and she will, doubtless, be able to assist your colleagues with that definition. Again, I don't read it. It's long, but I am grateful. So the Prosecution's assertion, that the 1984 convention, is settled law, no argument, finished, the end, can be seen in our submission as being really, not accurate. There is yet another definition for the want of, for just the sake of adding one, the UK law, although they're signatory to the 1984 convention, the act which imports that into English law and contains yet another definition of what torture is. It's slightly more elliptical, if I may use that. It's not the best piece of legislation that I have ever seen from the United Kingdom. I turn now quickly to wilfully causing great suffering there are three points. The use of the word wilful in that phrase, we submit that the mens rea that you apply to that should be consistent, indeed the same, as far as possible with any other definition of mens rea that you give to the word wilful. The second thing is we set out in our half-time submissions that the law of this offence lacked proper clarity, precision and accessibility of language. And say for those reasons, it breaches the principal of Nullum crimen sina lege (Latin). If that's not a proper -- if that's not right, the proper test is there must be a wilful act, which either cause great suffering or caused serious injury to health or body. Again, inhumane acts, we again say that we have set out a clear basis for saying that the laws there lack the required clarity, precision and accessibility of language in the half-time submissions. Indeed, the Pictet commentaries themselves plainly agree that this idea is rather difficult to define. And for a set of commentaries defines quite a lot of things, that says a lot. We say, again, there is a violation of the principle of Nullum crimen sina lege (Latin). I conclude with a short word about plunder. When I came last March, March 1997, that is, to work at this court and appear here before Your Honours, I little imagined that I was coming to the detention camp equivalent of shoplifting. Stealing watches and coins is not what plunder is about. It is not a serious grave breach of the Geneva Conventions. Plunder is what Herman Goering did with the art of Eastern Europe. That's what grave breaches are. Or, for example, emptying entire houses of their quality furniture. That's plunder. But stealing a watch and a few coins is not what we were brought and assembled at great expense to try in my submission. The evidence in this case is essentially that was what was stolen. It doesn't meet, by a very long way, those criteria. And we urge that that count in particular, as a matter of law, has no proper place in this Court. I think I have just about done twenty minutes and a bit. And I do apologise if I have gone on too long. Those are our submissions and we urge you to take them carefully into consideration.

But, our main submission is that we don't concede that it is the definition authored by the Prosecution. We've set it out at some length in the half-time submission. utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. After hearing the Prosecution case and the Defence case before this Trial Chamber, we hope, Your Honour, that we'll be able to present an assessment of the Defence as to whether the Prosecution has made a case against Mr. Zejnil Delalic, that is that he has committed the acts for which he has been indicted. The task of the honourable judges and the standard that you will certainly apply is that the accused can be found guilty only if there is evidence beyond any reasonable doubt and that standard is well known in all criminal procedures world-wide. If after carefully assessing all the evidence presented you ascertain that the Prosecutor has not done this, that is, has not borne the burden of proof in terms of proving all the key elements of the crimes mentioned in the indictment, then you will certainly have to release the defendant. In our law, as in all other laws, in dubio proraro is an universal principle of criminal law. In the case of Zejnil Delalic, I believe that your task is going to be quite easy. With full confidence in your experience of imminent legal expert and your human experience of lofty judges, I believe you will conscientiously and critically assess all the evidence presented. The only conclusion which you will reach, I believe, is that it is not only that the Prosecutor has proven beyond any reasonable doubt, not a single one of the counts in the indictment, against Zejnil Delalic, but on the contrary it has been established viva voce before this Court through hearing witnesses and on the basis of authentic and reliable documents, it has been ascertained that Zejnil Delalic not at a single point in time in the period mentioned in the indictment did not have a status of a superior in the prison of Celebici, over its staff, guards and other persons who allegedly committed the crimes in the indictment. May I recall the following, Your Honour. Counts 3 and 7 of the indictment, ascertains that Zejnil Delalic coordinated the forces of the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats in the territory of Konjic from April 1992 until September 1992 and that he was commander of Tactical Group No. 1 of the Bosinan forces sometime from June to November 1992 and in that capacity he was responsible for the work -- fort he functioning of the Celebici prison and he was, thus, a superior in relation to all the guards in the camp and all other individuals who came into the camp and mistreated the prisoners. I am not going to repeat the counts of the indictment because I know that you are fully aware of them, just as we are. Just one count, count 48, is the one that brings charges against Delalic for the unlawful confinement of civilians in keeping with Article 71(1) of the statute of the International Criminal Tribunal. In its written brief the Defence analysed in detail the legal and factual issues related to the subject matter of the indictment and the evidence presented. Therefore, today I shall briefly only draw your attention to some of these questions, notably those that are related to the status of the accused. A foremost question in terms of establishing responsibility in the sense of Article 7 of the statute of our Tribunal, that is a conditio sine qua non is that the accused person had the status of a superior person at all. What does the Prosecutor say about this? In the Pre-Trial brief of the 24th of February 1997 the Prosecutor took the position presented in the commentary of the ICRC on Protocol I of the Geneva Conventions, according to which the concept of a superior is a broader one and should be viewed within the context of the hierarchy that encompasses the concept of control, too. Today we have heard a broader concept. This concept of a superior person is being extended by the Prosecutor to every person which enjoyed a reputation in a given area and in this way reaches certain positions. This is the same position that was upheld in the introductory remarks of the Prosecutor, notably stating that evidence will show that Delalic had direct control over the perpetrators and their superiors in the Celebici prison, that he had direct control over the staff of the Celebici prison, that Delalic was officially in charge of the prison, that the prison was within the area of his command. The Prosecutor has not proven a single one of these allegations. Aware of the fact that he will not be able to present evidence on the official position of direct control of Delalic in the Celebici prison, the Prosecutor disassociated himself from this by stating the following: No matter what kind of arguments could be drawn on his de jure authority there is no doubt whatsoever that he had defacto responsibility over the Celebici prison. That is what was said today by the Prosecutor in her closing argument. Also, the Prosecutor reminds us of what they said earlier, too; perhaps others shared this authority, too. That is to say persons who delegated this responsibility to Delalic. But the fact is that others are responsible, and that is no defence for Delalic. However, this allegation was not proven by the Prosecutor, either. In respect to Delalic, the Prosecutor insists on an inaccurate and untenable assumption which reads as follows, according to the Prosecutor: Delalic is superior and responsible for the prison of Celebici, regardless of the status he had and what duties he performed in the period from May to November of 1992. That is to say that the Prosecutor believes that by extending the scope of responsibility for Delalic that it is all the same, whether he is an ordinary civilian, a rank in file soldier, a coordinator between the War Presidency and the Defence forces, or whether he is commander of Tactical Group 1. Because in each and every one of these statuses, according to the Prosecutor, Delalic is always superior in the Celebici prison. The Prosecutor opted for this assumption precisely because he could not prove that Delalic, as coordinator or as commander of Tactical Group 1, had any formal authority over the prison. So, the Prosecutor himself accepts that neither the coordinator nor the commander of Tactical Group 1 have authority over the prison. But as we heard today, Zejnil Delalic does, irrespective of his official status and authority. According to this thesis, it can be derived that Delalic was in charge of the -- would have been in charge of the prison, even had he not been the coordinator and the commander of Tactical Group 1. Precisely for that reason, through the evidence that he presented, the Prosecutor tried to create the feeling and conviction that Delalic in fact had great power and great personal influence over all institutions in Konjic and all the people around him. I think, Your Honours, that you will agree with me that this is an absolutely inaccurate and unrealistic claim. In the period for which Delalic is indicted, in Konjic there was a War Presidency as the main organ of civilian authority. The War Presidency of Konjic consisted of very influential, authoritative people from Konjic with a high reputation. At the same time there was a municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence. In addition to the commander, there were some 40 officers in it. Also there was a municipal staff of the HVO with a fully autonomous structure. In the critical period there was also a joint command of the Territorial Defence and the HVO with a developed system of command and with at least 30 officers on it who comprised this command. In Konjic at this time there was also a police MUP which was subordinated to the ministry in Sarajevo. So, as you have had ample opportunity to see and hear during this trial, in the institutions of civilian and military government in Konjic there was over 100 persons who held certain posts and authority and also had a personal reputation and dignity and a feeling of responsibility. In this area at that time there were also the representatives of the chief command, among them four generals, too; General Divjak, General Kadic, General Pasalic and General Polutak. Before this court three of these generals have testified. The president of the War Presidency, Dr. Hadzihuseinovic testified, as well, and the representative of the republican staff Brigadier Dzembasovic (Phoen). It is quite clear to everyone who heard and saw these people, that these are credible witnesses, that these are educated, able, decisive persons. Therefore, it is untenable to assume that Delalic had power over them and that they were subordinated to Delalic. These people held their civilian and military posts even before Delalic came to Konjic, and they continued to discharge their duties after Delalic left, too. May we recall the following: 20 years before the war Delalic lived outside of Konjic. He spent only eight months during the year of 1992 in Konjic. Therefore, it is not only unbelievable, but it is also impossible that after 20 years a person comes back to a town and that within a month's time he establishes a personal power of his own in that town and his own influence over hundreds of educated authoritative people with a high reputation, and if you wish, people who also have their vanity, and who are in high positions of civilian and military power. It would be incredible to believe Zejnil Delalic or anyone else who had the command responsibility of a superior would be hiding behind different names; but we heard from the commander of Desna Obala at that time it was an honour to be a commander. The Prosecution has presented its case, but did not manage to provide arguments, In paragraph 4.1119 of their final brief they themselves almost acknowledge that fact. I quote ” Although Delalic’s control and responsibility over the prison as a whole and over the prison , commander is not acceptable and even if the arguments presented by the Defence prove this, it is certain that he had sufficient authority in the prison, including authority to classify prisoners and release them. We have heard about many of these things before and we have said in detail what we had to say about this in our own written submission, but I shall say only briefly upon what we think the Prosecution bases its case on. First of all, these are several witness statements by people who did not know enough personally about Delalic and what kind of authority he had. Secondly, on the basis of witness statements by persons who cannot be trusted because of their personal status, and because they gave contradictory statements, and because of their attitude towards Delalic. So, these statements cannot have probative value. Thirdly, on the basis of the testimony of an expert witness who before this court admitted that he did not do any research on the situation in Konjic itself and that he bases his knowledge about this situation only on the documents that were made accessible to him by the Prosecution. Fourthly, on inauthentic and unreliable documents, which because of that and because of the inaccurate facts they contained, cannot have any probative value. I shall say something very briefly about this particular evidence. First of all, the witnesses of the Prosecution who were over a certain period of time prisoners in Celebici do not have any personal knowledge of the duties and responsibilities of Zejnil Delalic. Of course, Your Honours, on the basis of the testimony of these persons, you cannot ascertain what kind of authority and status Zejnil Delalic had. In contrast, numerous witnesses of the Defence, members of the civilian and military structures of Konjic, credible witnesses that are supported by numerous documents that they often presented themselves, are telling proof of his duties and authorities. Secondly, Witness D is one of the important witnesses upon which the Prosecutor proves his case; that is that Delalic had the status of a superior. This witness is contradictory in his own right and is not credible, and therefore, cannot serve as a basis for ascertaining any kind of position of Zejnil Delalic. His testimony has been brought into question by the statements made by many witnesses and authentic documents. If you remember the statement made by Witness D before this court, you will remember how greatly contradictory his own statement is. Actually, when speaking before you he did not even know when he came to Konjic and when he allegedly visited the house of Zejnil Delalic, and he gave several different versions of these events. He did not know when he started working in the military investigative commission. He was contradictory to such an extent on the allegedly held meeting in Celebici attended by Zejnil Delalic that there is reasonable doubt as to, it can be reasonably suspected as to whether such a meeting was ever held. Also, there is contradiction in terms of his testimony on writing the report on the conditions in the Celebici prison, in terms of the substance of this report and who this report was sent to. First he says that Delalic made these categories, and then after that he doesn't know who made these categories at all. He did not know anything about the document dated the 1st of June, which he allegedly got at the meeting with Delalic; and then during the course of his testimony about this same document and his reception, he gave a few different versions. What is certain is, which was proven by this witness before you, that he is from the HVO Mostar, that he was recommended and that he was in the HVO Konjic; that he reported at HVO Konjic and offered his services; that he was told to report to Goran Lokas, the president of the military investigative commission; that for the same reasons he was called by Miroslav Stenek and he was told to contact the HVO; that after this he was to report to Ivan Azinovic, the president of the HVO, which he subsequently did. And that he is quite sure that at that time it was only the HVO who could appoint Croats to certain duties. For this reason, it is quite, it cannot be understood that the Prosecutor can maintain and continue to maintain that Zejnil Delalic appointed Witness D to a particular appointment in the military investigative commission and explained to him the work he would have to do in the presence of the most responsible people of the HVO, Dinko Zebic, the commander of the HVO, and Ivan Azinovic the president of the HVO. Attempting to save the credibility of this witness in his written response dating back to March 1998, the Prosecutor attempts to convince us that the witness only has trouble in remembering dates, and he suggests that perhaps the document of the 1st of June sent to Ivan Azinovic was in fact given to Witness D either on occasion of the first meeting in the house of Zejnil Delalic forgetting in that regard that Witness D, according to his own testimony, went to that house precisely with Ivan Azinovic. And therefore, there would be no point in Zejnil Delalic writing a message for Azinovic in his presence. Or perhaps that this message was given to him when he came to take over his uniform, forgetting the fact that Witness D also gave contradictory testimony and said Zejnil Delalic at their first meeting promised him a uniform but the uniform was issued to him by somebody else and he signed for it. Witness D is not certain whether any document of this kind was given to him by Zejnil Delalic, and as he described earlier, circumstances whereby he received the document during the meeting with Delalic in Celebici, brings into question the meeting itself and the competency of Delalic upon which the Prosecution bases its allegations. What we know, or what we were able to become convinced in through this witness's testimony, is that he reported for duty at the HVO in Konjic; that his alleged knowledge on what had taken place in the Celebici camp was told to Ivan Azinovic, the president of the HVO and other responsible individuals of the HVO; that Ivan Azinovic allegedly told him to cease performing his duty, which he did immediately. That a report, according to his personal knowledge, was sent exclusively to the HVO, and before you, Your Honours, he stated that he had never seen an original copy, that he signed a copy, and that he doesn't know to whom that report was sent or whether it was sent to anybody else. The credibility of every witness, and this witness as well, is another important question that this Trial Chamber will have to deliberate. And I'm sure the question will arise as to why Witness D would have to accuse Delalic. Perhaps it would be well for me to remind you of the testimony of Regis Abribat, who testified before this Trial Chamber. He said that during investigations on the Celebici case no criminal report existed against Zejnil Delalic on the part of any state or international organisation, and that their investigation led to a reasonable doubt as to Zejnil Delalic's crimes. The statements, according to which the indictment was confirmed, were based on the testimony of Ivan Azinovic and Mladen Zebic, who did not appear before this Trial Chamber. From the testimony of Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic and Dzevad Pasic we were able to learn that as early on as 1992 they were the protagonists of a campaign against Zejnil Delalic asserting he was a Chetnik and a traitor. Ivan Azinovic was head of Witness D, who belongs to the same circle of individuals. In this connection, and in connection with this witness, let me remind you of the testimony made by Ziad Salihamidzic, who knew Witness D since before the war as a worker in the state security institution. In 1992 Witness D asked Salihamidzic allegedly compromising data on General Jovo Divjak and Zejnil Delalic. Evidence placed before this Trial Chamber showed that because of allegations of this kind Jovo Divjak was arrested, and a relentless campaign was waged against Zejnil Delalic. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will take into account all these facts put before you when you come to your deliberations as to the credibility of the witness. I am fully aware of this. However, independently of the reasons put forward as to the credibility of this witness, it is far more important that other witnesses which we have also heard before this Trial Chamber, members of the staff and War Presidency and internal affairs organs, Kevric, Cerovac, Tahirovic, Duracic, and Dzumhur Hadzihuseinovic were completely adamant in their assertion that Zejnil Delalic had no authorisation to appoint members of the military investigative committee and that he was not superior to it, that he could not appoint Croats to any office whatsoever, as he could not appoint Witness D; that he had no authorisation for the detention, imprisonment and keeping individuals in prison, nor did he have authorisation to free them. The statements of these credible witnesses bring into doubt the statements made by Witness D on all the relevant facts. The majority of the evidence upon which the Prosecutor bases his views as regards Zejnil Delalic's responsibilities in the concluding brief are connected to video-tapes and documents which were found in the INDA-BAU company in Vienna. Of specific importance in assessing this evidence is the decision made by Your Honours in this Trial Chamber in connection with the weight to be attached to the so-called Vienna documents. In that respect, I think that it is a good idea for us to recall the following paragraph; trials between international courts are led by professional judges, which according to their experience and knowledge are able to evaluate every piece of evidence presented and to assess its probative value. As has been stated, it is implicitly provided by the rules that the Trial Chamber should give all attention to the reliability evidence when deciding upon its admissibility. However, this kind of terminology could leave space for a lack of understanding or different interpretations that in this stage of the proceedings, the origins and authorship of the evidence is presented. And therefore, the Trial Chamber would like to make it clear that the acceptance of documents as evidence does not mean that the statements will necessarily show an exact explanation of the facts as they stand. Factors such as authenticity and proof of authorship will have a great importance when the Trial Chamber comes to assess each of the individual pieces of evidence submitted. In addition to that, Your Honours, the weight of every piece of evidence whose authors did not appear as witnesses will be dealt with if they did not appear in the cross-examination. The Defence considers that this stand presented in the decision mentioned should be a standard in appraising evidence in this hearing, particularly those with regard to Zejnil Delalic, whether we are talking about Defence evidence or Prosecution evidence. So that, we could then go to archives to determine the authenticity of the evidence if we were to determine somebody's responsibility. We have spoken a great deal about the Vienna documents in written arguments. Relying on Dr. Gow's expert testimony, the Prosecution says that there was a vacuum in Konjic and relations were not regulated, and because the district headquarters in links with Sarajevo, that Konjic had a great degree of autonomy, and that in a situation of this kind Zejnil Delalic, according to his personal ability and political influence, had de facto authority and authorisations in the municipality. These assertions are without basis in the evidence provided. We heard the First and Seventh commander of the municipal headquarters, 21 members of staff, and the joint commanands together with the chiefs of staff, and we also heard the commanders and Sadic Dzumhur, the deputy of the head of MUP, Brigadier Dzambasovic and Vasogic, and Dzambasovic who on behalf of the supreme command was located in Konjic at that time. For Zejnil Delalic to be in a position of superiority, he must have been a member of one civilian or military authority. All the witnesses that we listened to said that Zejnil, as a coordinator, was not a member of either a civilian authority or military authorities. Nor did those authorities give him any competencies over the prison itself. Zejnil Delalic had no authorisation over the prison, either when he was commander of the tactical group or at any other time. The Prosecutor states that in William Lists trials in the United States of America and so forth, he tries to make us realise that Zejnil Delalic has the authorisation of a regional commander. However, it is precisely this decision that determines that the question of subordination of the units for criminal liability becomes important in the case when the competency of the commander is tactical. And everything showed that the authorisation of Zejnil Delalic was exclusively tactical. The witnesses from Jablanica, Prozor, Hadzici, Konjic 21 and elsewhere clearly show that Zejnil Delalic, as commander of the tactical group was never in superiority over the formations of the armed forces of the municipality. And for this reason, the assertion of the Prosecution which relies on the appointment of the 27th, whereas Zejnil took over his duties on the 30th, is absolutely refuted by all the testimony that ensued. The errors in appointment, or placing it at actor, came eight days after that. The Prosecutor insists on certain parts of an order dating to the 24th and 28th of August, and stating that, maintaining that Zejnil Delalic was superior to the commander of the municipal headquarters, Esad Ramic, and the Prosecutor said so today. The Prosecutors brought under subpoena Esad Ramic and decided not to listen to him. That he, Esad Rasmic, could tell the Prosecutor that Zejnil Delalic was superior in this period when he was coordinator, or when he was acting as commander of TG, 14 Prosecutor would have brought forward this individual. Esad Ramic was not able to confirm this. Had he come into this courtroom in October, this would have been exculpatory importance. Today the Prosecutor tells us that he has no direct proof, but if we link up some small elements of proof, that case can be built up against Zejnil Delalic. In this way, he has tried to build up his knowledge about the events that took place, because he did not succeed in proving his authority over the prison and the prison staff. All the facts prove that Zejnil Delalic, up to the 18th of May, was a civilian, and that from the 18th of May to the 27th of June was the coordinator as a civilian between the war time presidency and the defence forces without any rank and that as commander of Tactical Group 1, from the 30th of July, had no competencies over the prison, the staff and the wardens or the guards in that prison. Linking up individual parts to show that Zejnil Delalic knows something of the events that took place in the prison, the Prosecutor in 0.411, indicates some of that proof that comes under the knowledge of Zejnil Delalic. The Defence maintains that Zejnil Delalic did not know and did not have reason to know what was going on and that the crimes in Celebici had taken place and been committed. As the Prosecution cannot prove this in the count mentioned, the Prosecution maintains that witness D for many months after leaving Celebici, met Mrs. Jasna Dzumhur, president of the commission, and that on that occasion, she said I informed Delalic about everything and nothing more. Therefore, Witness D and Jasna never stated what they discussed, in fact. Because everything means nothing, is the same as nothing. And, at the same time, nobody said what Jasna Dzumhur knows about events in Celebici. Let's us remind you that Witness D did not know a lot of this. He knew of the death of Mrkajic, that he had died of diabetes. If we look at the quality of these assertions and allegations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Make sure that you are keeping your eye to the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I have been informed that I have five minutes and I shall be winding up within those five minutes. If that information is incorrect, then I have overstepped my time limit and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you haven't, but conclude your address.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, the alleged knowledge on the part of third persons and statements to journalists at Television Sarajevo, as his knowledge on the events in Celebici, the general knowledge on the crimes which was not confirmed by interrogations of any of the witnesses, these individual portions on the basis of which the Prosecutor wishes to show that Zejnil Delalic could have certain responsibilities and could have had certain knowledge. Your Honours, as the basic element for establishing responsibility of a superior via a brief analysis of this and other evidence provided by us has not ascertained beyond any reasonable doubt. On the contrary, it has asserted that Zejnil Delalic, neither as a coordinator nor as commander of the said Tactical Group belonged to any of the organs or structures which had competency and authority over the prison. On the other hand, these bodies and structures did not give Zejnil Delalic any authorisation of this kind. Therefore, no prerequisites exist for establishing responsibility on the basis of Article 7(3), Zejnil Delalic should be acquitted of all the charges as brought against him and the counts in the indictment. In the written arguments and in our witness brief, we expound the other elements. But, for purposes of caution, questions of knowledge, I think that these arguments are sufficient to ascertain that Zejnil did not have any reasonable possibility of the criminals. The last murder was committed at the end of July, whereas Zejnil Delalic had no knowledge of the perpetration of any of the crimes listed in the indictment. The last thing that I wish to say is that in our written brief, we set out in detail responsibility according to Article 7(1), Zejnil Delalic was not, nor did personally detained or imprisoned or maintained in confinement any civilians. In that sense, the Prosecutor has not provided any evidence and has not proved beyond any shadow of doubt, and as he did not do so, I propose that Zejnil Delalic be acquitted of all the counts in the indictment and charges brought against him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we now hear the address of counsel for Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, esteemed counsel, this trial began over 18 months ago. During that time many faces have changed on both sides of counsel table. On behalf of our client, Mr. Mucic, I thank all of you for your patience, for your time and the seriousness with which you have taken your duties as honoured judges in this Tribunal. We also thank the support staff, the registry, the victim witnesses unit, the interpreters for dealing with us, our problems and the case. They should all be publicly acknowledged. Without them, none of this would go. I would also like to -- having to keep in mind the final submissions, one of my law professors once told me when it came to examinations, I read them I don't weigh them. So keep that in mind when meeting our final submission. It is, roughly, a hundred pages. A large number of witnesses have given testimony in this case. There have been hundreds of documents submitted into evidence. Mr. Moran had mentioned at one point in time during the trial that Judge Jan promised counsel that everyone would be home by Christmas. Unfortunately, it was never confirmed in what year that promise could be fulfilled. Nonetheless, all good things must come to an end. We are now at the end. There are two overriding issues we ask you to keep in your mind throughout these closings. When you deliberate on issues of fact and on issues of law, the burden of proof and witness credibility. With respect to the former, Mr. Mucic submits that the Prosecution, despite attempts from all angles, has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Mucic had command authority over Celebici and all the things that flow from that authority. With respect to the later, Mr. Mucic submits that the credibility of the witnesses upon whom the Prosecution relies the most in their case against him, Witness D and co-accused, Mr. Esad Landzo, to name but two, lack credibility. Later in this closing, I will demonstrate how this credibility is lacking. The Prosecution in its closing statement said that this is a case of the accused absolving himself of responsibility. We strongly disagree. The real issue is, what is that responsibility? Is it defined? Does it have any parameters? What is a commander in Celebici? Inherent in attempting to prove that a commander has imputed criminal responsibility as having command. In this case, after proof of command, must come proof of knowledge of unlawful subordinate conduct by commander. This must then be followed by proof of power to deter, investigate and punish unlawful conduct, not based on a commander's orders. We submit that not one witness put forth by the Prosecution has given evidence beyond a reasonable doubt to any of those proofs and parameters. Essentially, the elements of command responsibility. Command authority cannot come from thin air. The Prosecution's position is that Mr. Mucic was the commander because people have said, even second and third hand that he was the commander. That begs the question, what is the commander? There is certainly a reasonable doubt on who was the commander. The Court must be aware of the uncertainty as to who was, in fact, the commander or administrator or warden, whatever term is used of Celebici in May, June and July 1992. The Court itself through the Honourable Judge Karibi-Whyte asked this question of a Defence witness, Mr. Sadik Dzumhur and I'll quote it: "QUESTION: Do you, by the way, know the person who was in charge of the persons in Celebici? Who was the head at that time? "ANSWER: What period of time? "QUESTION: Up to June 15, 1992, once perhaps you ceased to go there. "ANSWER: Until June the 15th, I know that a MUP unit was accommodated in Celebici and that heading that unit was Rale Musinovic. "QUESTION: And you know that the MUP was in charge of the prisoners? They were looking after the prisoners detained there? "ANSWER: In that period, yes." There is evidence in the case that suggest a number of other possibilities. The first being that Rale Musinovic was the commander for at least part of that time. There is no evidence that Mr. Mucic was member of the MUP. Dzevad Alibasic is another candidate. Witness D is one as well. Similarly, it is unclear which authority controlled the detainee section of the camp at certain times in 1992. There are several possibilities. MUP, HVO, TO or a combination of all or some of these. None of the lines are clear, all of the lines are blurred. And none has been put in focus by the Prosecution's magnifying glass. It has never been demonstrated where the ultimate authority lay and from whom any person in Celebici derived their authority. In these circumstances, it is not possible to say what authority Mr. Mucic had and how Mr. Mucic could exercise that authority beyond a reasonable doubt. First, many military, paramilitary and police units plainly had easy and frequent access to the camp for a multitude reasons. Defence witness Dzumur and defence witness Emir Dzajic clearly reveal the variety of units present there and a number of persons who are candidates for command of the personnel there through July 1992. Mr. Mucic had no rank, belonged in no police, military or paramilitary organisation. I don't think there is a dispute there. Second, there is consistent evidence that other units who plainly had nothing to do with Mr. Mucic would come into the camp and occasionally wreak havoc. The MUP units led by the likes of Jasmin Guska, who was the head of the unit, and Sefko Mucici, the deputy commander come to mind. Given the ability of these units to enter Celebici freely, it has not been demonstrated how anyone, much less Mr. Mucic, had the power to control these entities or entries or to investigate and punish such units. Bearing in mind that the later unit mentioned was itself a military police unit. If the military police itself perpetrated crimes, to whom was Mr. Mucic or anyone, for that matter, expected to make a report of their crimes? Given these circumstances, a person such as Mr. Mucic who was prepared, and there is evidence to take risks of helping Bosnian Serbs to escape to Bosnia Serb control territory, must inevitably fall back on his own personal, moral authority. In the kiosk that was Konjic, Celebici and Bosnia-Herzegovina itself at the time. It was the power of his personality and not any unproven power invested by him by someone the Prosecution has not put on the witness stand that carried the day. At the end of July, 1992, the situation in Celebici turned around dramatically. The bulk of the serious incidents alleged by the Bosnian/Serb witnesses happened in May, June or July. By contrast, although there are some allegations of crimes after the end of July, the general picture of the camp was of an escalating program of transfers to Musala and other outright releases. Now, there is no dispute that Mr. Mucic was in the camp before the end of July, but such presence in and of itself does not prove or indicate that he was at that given moment, the commander or the administrator or the warden or whatever kind of term you want to put to Mr. Mucic. It has already been pointed out that entry into the camp by those that had no function there was relatively easy to achieve. His presence there may well have been either in a personal capacity or in the exercise of some other function, unconnected with the command or administrative hierarchy of the camp. By the way, the Prosecution has failed to disprove that his position was in either of those capacities. In the absence of written documentation of appointment to the position of commander or administrator or warden, it cannot be proved at what date he took over such a position and what powers and duties emanated from Mr. Mucic by such an appointment. The burden of proof, which, as the Court will recall, was the first of two themes I asked the Court to keep in mind at the beginning of the closing argument. It revolves around the phrase, beyond a reasonable doubt. This phrase is codified in the rules of the tribunal, specifically Rule 87(a). And I quote, "A finding of guilt may be reached only when a majority of the Trial Chamber is satisfied that guilt has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt." One American court in Massachusetts in 1850 in what is now known as the traditional definition of this phrase in American jurisprudence, defined it as "That state of the case, which, after the entire comparison and consideration of all the evidence, leaves the minds of jurors in that condition that they cannot say they feel an abiding conviction to a moral certainty and the truth of the charge."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic submits that after the entire comparison and consideration of all the evidence in this case, that this honourable Tribunal cannot, to paraphrase that case, feel an abiding conviction to a moral certainty of the truth of the charges in the indictment against Mr. Mucic. The second issue I ask the Court to keep in mind is the issue of credibility of witnesses. The Prosecution in their final written submissions advance their case on the basis that each and every one of their witnesses was telling the truth at all times and that none of their credibility was impeached. At best, we think such an approach is misleading. Mr. Moran pointed out too numerous examples, which I will not cover again, of how some witnesses were to be hopelessly untruthful. Mr. Vukalo was one example. Another example was the Witness T, Mrs. Cecez's, digression. There are numerous other examples of witnesses who were properly impeached by similar means or in other ways. This trial has particular significance in the context of various conflict in the former Yugoslavia. One which was established by the prosecution itself when settling this indictment and is one which creates a positive incentive for untruthful evidence to be given. On March 22nd of 1996 the ICTY announced the first indictment of four alleged perpetrators of crimes against Bosnian Serb victims. Whether it was intended or not, this emphasis by the OTP, "On the first indictment dealing with Bosnian Serbs," immediately made it a case for political significance for the Bosnian Serbs and for the Serbs. Until that time, the subject of the indictments have been largely, if not exclusively, Serbs or Bosnian Serbs. In this propaganda war which ensued, it was plainly important for there to be presented a picture of atrocities against Bosnian/Serbs or Serbs to counter or deflect the impression that only war criminals were from such a background. It is evident that the prosecution had to rely on a Serb refugee organisation to put some of its case together as well. In assessing the credibility of witnesses, we submit that the Trial Chamber should at all times be alert to this fact and bear in mind the significant degree of involvement in this case of that Serb refugee organisation. Their view of the world was clearly demonstrated by the medical notes kept by Witness O, a prominent member of that association, who with frequent references to examining Bosnian Serbs, who had been in an Ustasha camp, clearly reveals the agenda that was being pursued. Mr. Moran mentioned the old axiom truth is the first causality of war. Given the opportunity incentive that the trial presents to Bosnian Serb or Serb elements to influence or described on one occasion as "our witnesses," was during Witness O's TV interview with a Serb TV station in June of 1997. Evidence of "our witnesses" has to be approached with even more care than is usual in a situation such as this. The issue of credibility also arises in relation to the co-accused, Esad Landzo. Two points here: Point one, it has been quite clearly demonstrated that he is a witness who is incapable of being treated as a credible witness. It is quite obvious that he is a person who may lie at any time and who may, if he considers that such lies would help to save his skin, do so. He has claimed that he was prepared to lie at the suggestion of his first counsel, Mr. Brackovic, who allegedly advised him to blame Mr. Mucic because Mr. Mucic was a Bosnian Croat and not a Bosnian Muslim. He has clearly told lies to those who have been investigating events at Celebici. He has now made allegations against both Mr. Delic and Mr. Mucic about their alleged influence over him while at Celebici. We believe that he does not have credibility and that his evidence should be disregarded. Point two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We may have a break at this stage and resume at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As you recall, before the break there were two questions I wanted to mention with respect to Mr. Landzo's testimony on credibility; first point being Mr. Landzo's voracity. Point two is this: More curious and quite puzzling is that the Prosecution in their final written submission seeks to invite the Trial Chamber to rely upon Mr. Landzo as a witness of the truth. Later in the same document they seek to impeach him as witness whose evidence is not credible. The Prosecution should not be allowed to have it both ways, either he is credible or he isn't. And it's closing submission, written submission, the Prosecution referred to the Pohl case when speaking of Mr. Mucic. Karl Mummenthey, as if drawing a comparison between him and the crimes he committed and Mr. Mucic. That case concerned those who had had a part in the management of concentration camps and slave labour under the Nazi administration in Germany. There is a huge distinction between that case, a case where the defendants knowingly set out to participate in the Nazi programme of extermination and slavery, rather than the case of Celebici, which was turned from a military supply depot into an ad hoc detention facility on short notice under all the exigencies and the onset of war in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We believe this is a fairly gratuitous reference which has misjudged the role and nature of Mr. Mucic and the essential characteristics of the camp. As much as the Prosecutor wants to convict Mr. Mucic, we believe this comparison is wrong. We see no more about this attempt to characterise Mr. Mucic as an evil man, as quoted in the brief, other than it is completely inappropriate. There is, of course, quite a different side to Mr. Mucic, and it's worth remembering some of the observations made by witnesses who testified here, Mr. Golubovic being one, who have accurately assessed Mr. Mucic as a human being. On page 2197 of the transcript the question was put to Mr. Golubovic, "Do you remember saying this to the OTP, quote, if at least 20 per cent of people of Bosnia were like Mucic, there would have been no war?" End quote. "Answer: I remember that. That is what I said. "Question: That is a fair remark, is it not, Mr. Golubovic? "Answer: Yes, it is, I think that still. This man was a Prosecution witness put forward by the Prosecution as someone upon whom you could rely. In considering the man, Mr. Mucic, it is better to look at the evidence about him rather than gratuitous remarks which compare him with one of the notorious Nazi war criminals tried at Nuremberg at the end of the second World War. Also in the words of Nedeljko Draganic (Phoen) at 1694 of the transcript: "What you told in the investigators was this, that Pavo Mucic enjoyed a good reputation in the community as a fair and good man. That is in your statement, that is what you were telling the investigators in October 1995. Do you accept that?" "Answer: Yes, I said that. And later, on 1701: "Question: It is for these reasons that we have been discussing just now that you have a good reason to thank Mr. Mucic. "Answer: Yes. "Question: And to be grateful to him for having, as you acknowledged, saved the life of not just yourself, but in fact your family. "Answer: Yes." This reputation for helping the Bosnian Serbs, in addition to evidence of him inhibiting activities, must be viewed against the background of evidence of Witness D on pages 5408 through 5410 of the transcript. I think this is very significant, Your Honours, with respect to Witness D. The question was posed to him: "Can you help us? You were aware of the existence of representatives of international bodies in the Konjic area, were you, at the time this was taking place?" "Answer: UNHCR was definitely there among the international organisations. I don't know where their premises were. The international Red Cross, I don't know if they were in Konjic. "Question: Did you make any attempt to bring your concerns about Celebici camp to their attention? "Answer: I did not try to do that, and frankly, I didn't even know where to go. But I wasn't thinking of that. I was thinking about what we were doing and what we should be doing. Unfortunately, I have to say that I did not say everything that I could have done, speaking from where I speak now, today. You know afterwards, you see that you didn't do everything that you could have done at the time, unfortunately. "Question: Was one of your concerns if you had been seen to do that, to report matters to international bodies, that would have been seen as helping Chetniks? "Answer: You asked a very good question. That speaks of the situation that I described before we had the break for lunch. "Question: To be perceived as helping Chetniks, you have told us, would be a dangerous thing for your health. "Answer: Of course. Not only mine. "Question: But certainly that was your perception, that there was danger in it. "Answer: That is a different issue. It was dangerous to offer assistance, and the danger came from those elements, who without thinking clearly or reasonably, simply hatred arose among them, that everybody should be hated in general, and then you could encounter such people that could do just anything to you without thinking." This is important uncontroversial evidence from Witness D. What it indicates is it was dangerous for one's personal safety to be seen or thought of as helping quote, "Chetniks", end quote, which it may be accepted was the prevailing atmosphere at the time. The Prosecution gave this witness a glowing testimonial, which in light of Defence evidence presented about his role, may be seen as inaccurate. But according to the Prosecution, Witness D was such a good man, despite the fact that he took no steps to report facts which he claimed had come to his attention about crimes to the police, or to international humanitarian bodies. Now, the situation was not any different for Mr. Mucic. Even if he had command authority, he would have faced at least the same problems as D, if not more so. If an experienced and senior ex-secret policeman felt he did not have the knowledge or ability to make more report about these matters, the Prosecution have not shown why and to what extent Mr. Mucic's position was any different. It may be well thought to be common sense that to be seen as a friend of the Bosnian Serbs would have brought about repercussions for Mr. Mucic that would have seriously inhibited his ability to exercise any power he had to protect the detainees. It may well be that Mr. Mucic had no more power to do so than his own moral force to inhibit or prevent mistreatment. It has not been proven whether he was a military commander or a civilian warden or administrator and it certainly has not been proven in either case what powers were given to him to investigate and punish those who mistreated detainees. In the absence of such proof, it is not possible to say that he had any power to punish. But the weight of the evidence is that whatever his undefined power was, he could not exercise it in any way since he could not get beyond the first step of identifying the perpetrator. If he was unable to identify who had done it, he could not have done anything to punish or would not have had anyone to report to. I would like to now briefly focus the Court's attention to some issues of law. On the nationality issue we rely on what amounts to an admission that the persons alleged in the indictment were somehow, quote, "non-nationals", end quote, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were in fact of Bosnian nationality, contained in paragraph 2 of the indictment. Think about this for a moment, Mr. Moran mentioned it: It's very simple but very compelling. Why are they called Bosnian Serbs? Because they are Bosnian. The Prosecution describes those who were detained at Celebici as Bosnian Serbs, which amounts to a clear and unambiguous identification by the Prosecution of the nationality of the detainees as Bosnian which no amount of legal limbo can undo. It is not a distinction without a difference. Exhibit 130, in their written submission the Prosecution relies on it as if it was proved it was a document created and signed by Mr. Mucic. There is no evidence this document was signed by Mr. Mucic. It will be recalled that the Prosecution was not permitted to prove the letter allegedly written by him to a witness. A consequence of that decision is there is no evidence from a handwriting expert that Exhibit 30 was signed by Mr. Mucic. It is, therefore, we believe, misleading to treat it as though it was proven to be signed by him. It was not found in his possession, it was never put to him in any interview and has never been acknowledged by him. And no one from the Bosnian embassy was brought in to authenticate the document. There is no evidence which proves it is his document. As to the Vienna documents generally, we rely on the arguments of the defence of Zejnil Delalic throughout this trial and in their closings. With respect to other general allegations in the indictment, the Prosecution has failed, we believe, to prove this was an international armed conflict, or if there was an international armed conflict, that the fighting in the Konjic Municipality had a sufficient nexus to that conflict to make the events in that municipality part of the international armed conflict. We rely on the argument of the others there, as well. Mr. Mucic, on the Article 3 charges, would refer the Court to Mr. Greaves' discussion and to the final submissions for the analysis there. In summary, the Prosecution has failed to prove its case against Mr. Mucic. There is no credible evidence he took part in any act of mistreatment. There is no credible, reliable evidence that he witnessed any mistreatment that would fall within the definition of murder, torture, causing great sufferings or serious injury or inhumane or cruel treatment as discussed by Mr. Greaves. There is no credible, reliable evidence that he knew in advance that any act of mistreatment was going to take place or that he had any duty or even any veil of authority to punish or prevent such acts. There is no evidence as to what authority or power he possessed. It is not proven that he had the power and authority to investigate and punish anyone; therefore, he can't be said to have properly failed to investigate and punish those over whom he had no authority. There is no credible, reliable evidence that proves what Mr. Mucic's position at Celebici was or what his authority was beyond a reasonable doubt. The Prosecution has failed in its burden of proof. We therefore ask this Honourable Tribunal to return a not guilty verdict on each count of this indictment for Mr. Mucic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I point out an error in the transcript? During his submissions Mr. Kuzmanovic mentioned Mr. Delic, and the transcript mentions Mr. Delalic on page 109 of Live Note, line 18. Line 18 reads "made allegations against Mr. Delalic and Mr. Mucic," and I believe Mr. Kuzmanovic said "against Mr. Delic and Mr. Mucic." I ask that that be corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed Mrs. McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Thank you, Your Honours. I'm Cynthia McMurrey, and along with Nancy Boler and Calvin Saunders, we represent Esad Landzo. This, the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, is completing the first multi-defendant war crimes trial ever attempted under this genesis of an innovative new law, and it's aimed at controlling the way that we participate in war. It's aimed at controlling and instilling a conscience on the world as we see it today. This is a real, a very noble goal. The multi-national character of these proceedings forces this Tribunal to construct a set of principles that are not familiar to any one advocate or one jurist. We all came in here, I know how uncomfortable it was at first, because we were all unsure about what laws applied; but we're coming out of this in a comfortable way. We know what to expect when we come to the proceedings now. We don't have an absolute definition of what the law is at this point, but I'm proud to be a part of being here and constructing this new foundation for international criminal law, and I want to thank this Court and I want to thank the Registry, and I want to thank the Victim and Witnesses Unit and security, and all of you for putting up with us and being very understanding and helping us solve our problems. As my colleague, Mr. Kuzmanovic, mentioned a while ago, the political motivations apparent in the Celebici case sprang from the fact that the Prosecutor must prove to the international community that she is interested in administering even-handed justice. This was her purpose stated in the Celebici indictment. Even-handed justice is both a sword and a shield, and for reasons of equity, example and precedent, this Tribunal must not tolerate a manipulation of this even-handed justice. Then there is no justice. Although the statute of this Tribunal is attempting to create individual responsibility for crimes stated in Article 2 through Article 5, the aim of the founders of customary international law was that this Tribunal should be focused on persons or governments acting with authority for such crimes. The Prosecutor of this very Tribunal, Louise Arbour, has given support to this limitation on prosecution by entering into an agreement with the government of Rwanda. The agreement is that only persons with authority or command responsibility will be tried in the International Tribunal for Rwanda. All the others will be tried and continue to be tried in the National Court. This double standard for justice verges on hypocrisy to have the Prosecutor in the Rwandan Tribunal say they will concentrate on people with authority and do absolutely the opposite here in this Tribunal with a young guard named Esad Landzo. Last month we had various members of all the members of the United Nations meeting in Rome to promulgate the rules to set up a permanent international criminal court. The Rome statute was adopted on July 17th. One of the main arguments put forth in the forum in Rome contends if a statute of the permanent court is allowed to remain so broad, the permanent court will become a dumping ground for all the complaints. A line must be drawn, and Louise Arbour has drawn that line with the Tribunal, and she is continuing to draw that line by recently dismissing the indictments against 16 Serb detainees accused of war crimes. Her reasons were consistent with an agreement of the Rwandan Tribunal. At the moment it is not possible to maintain complex separate trials for such connected acts committed by the accused who could be tried in the appropriate way, also in the national state courts. Mrs. Arbour recites procedural economy and excessive expenses as further reasons for dismissal. It was also stated that the Tribunal wants to separate the big fish from the small fish. Esad Landzo was targeted for Prosecution for three reasons: One, the Prosecution needed to display an example of prosecuting a Bosnian Muslim. Two, he voluntarily surrendered upon request, driving to Sarajevo and turning himself in to custody. And three, he is the token guard that the witnesses can now identify, because he's the one here on trial. In construing the statute of the Tribunal, history and experience outweigh logic. A bright line is drawn between those who incite and those who act out of a blood borne loyalty, misguided though it may be, to those they see as their kin. It is the calculated and cultivated culture of inhumanity at which world opinion aims, not the nameless guard who becomes infected with the virus. In our world among people who share the notion of civility and common decency, there is a shared perception that those who conceive, plan and execute crimes against humanity should be caught and punished. From such high convictions this Tribunal draws its strength. It shouldn't be squandered on the pursuit of common ordinary soldiers or prison guards. The Celebici case represents the first assertion of the Defence of diminished mental responsibility. This defence, if proven by a preponderance of the probabilities, will result in a finding that Esad Landzo was not guilty of the allegations of murder in the Celebici camp. Ms. McHenry may view this defence as a joke, but there is a lot more to it than getting butted in the head by a billy goat. The evidence presented by the mental health experts, Prosecution and Defence, supports the fact that Esad Landzo was suffering from a severe personality disorder from the time he was a very young boy. He was sickly, asocial and dependent. Overlap this basic personality disorder with post-traumatic stress disorder, PTSD, and what is created is a state of mind which results in diminished mental responsibility. The triggering trauma adding up to the PTSD was Esad Landzo's forced participation in a Croatian military training camp in March, April or May of 1991. Anyone, much less an 18-year-old boy, who was forced to sit in a room and be instructed how to effectively slit a human being's throat in front of him and participate in that while watching video-tapes of what crimes were being committed on the civilians in the area, would suffer a trauma. The mental health experts demonstrated how Esad Landzo was unable to exercise his own free will in the Celebici barracks in 1992. The credibility of the Prosecution witnesses who testified is surely suspect. As Mr. Moran and Mr. Kuzmanovic have already cited, although he didn't mention a name, when an association such as the association of detainees in Belgrade is allowed to hold testifying seminars and allowed to have a representative in the courtroom every day the evidence is presented, there is injustice. That representative sat here in the courtroom every day and reported back to the association of detainees what the testimony was, what the cross-examination was. Of course they could get their stories straight. And much of the evidence presented by these witnesses reflected the use of the same terms over and over again. The conclusion that is relied upon by this defence is simple. The Prosecutor has failed to present sufficient evidence to allow a rational trier of fact to find all evidence, all elements of every count or series of counts beyond a reasonable doubt; and two, has failed to present sufficient evidence to show a violation of international law by this Tribunal. At this point, so I'm not going to reiterate all the arguments, the Defence of Esad Landzo wishes to adopt the legal arguments put forth by Mr. Moran as far as international armed conflict goes, protected person, Common Article 3, and the arguments by Mr. Greaves as far as our submissions on intentional killing and torture, which I hope to have a definition for Judge Jan when we come back for rebuttal. The accused in the -- in fact, Mr. Moran did an excellent job simplifying these very complicated legal issues so that I think everybody could understand them. And now, the burden is beyond a reasonable doubt, not like it was at the half-time motion, though. Article 21.3 mandates that the accused shall be presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. And this Trial Chamber is well aware of the higher burden, that there is no higher burden allowed under law. This Trial Chamber must now review the allegations against Esad Landzo, as set forth by the Prosecutor in the indictment, and decide whether the Prosecution has proven each and every allegation beyond a reasonable doubt. We believe they have not. As I've been describing, whether you title it selective prosecution or you title it tokenism, a selective prosecution is one brought for reasons that are forbidden by governing law. In the United States there exists a strong body of legal jurisprudence to defend against selective prosecution. The decision to prosecute may not be based on any unjustifiable standard, such as race, religion or other arbitrary classification. In order to effectively assert selective prosecution, a defendant must make a threshold showing that the Prosecution declined to prosecute similarly situated suspects of other races or religions -- INTERPRETER: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: -- and that the defendant was singled out for prosecution on the basis of race or religion. Considering the following, the burden described above has most certainly been met.
