Now, I'm going to ask that this Court please have some tolerance for this. I'm going to try to use the ELMO in conjunction with my final argument. So, at this point, would you put number 1 up, please? Notwithstanding the proof that in the ICTR for Rwanda, the Prosecutor maintains an agreement that the Rwandan government, to prosecute only those accused who are considered big fish, she continues to support this policy here. On April 28th, 1998 in the Prosecutor versus Sikirica, S-I-K-I-R-I-C-A, case number 95-8 here, the Prosecutor, Louise Arbour, sealed the precedent that ordinary soldiers, or those without command responsibility, should not be prosecuted in this international forum. In these legal documents and in her statement made by the Prosecutor following the withdrawal of the charges against the accused, Mrs. Arbour concluded: "In light of that situation, I have re-evaluated," and I'm quoting, "re-evaluated all outstanding indictments, vis-à-vis the overall investigative and prosecutorial strategies of my office. Consistent with those strategies which involve maintaining an investigative focus on persons holding higher levels of responsibility are those who have been personally responsible for the exceptionally brutal or otherwise extremely serious offences -- INTERPRETER: Could the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: -- to withdraw the charges against a number of accused in what has been known as the Omarska and Keraterm indictments which were confirmed in February and July of 1995. This decision was taken in an attempt to balance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you hear the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you hear them? Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Hit me. This decision was taken in an attempt to balance the available resources within the Tribunal and in recognition of the need to prosecute cases fairly and expeditiously. I wish to emphasise that this decision is not based on lack of evidence in respect of these accused. I do not consider it feasible this time the hold multiple separate trials for related offences committed by perpetrators who could appropriately be tried in another judicial forum such as a state court. Esad Landzo steps clearly into these shoes of the 14 accused dismissed by the Prosecutor because she wishes to maintain an investigative focus on persons holding higher levels of responsibility and for fiscal economy. All of the accused whose indictments have been dismissed by the Prosecutor are of Serb ethnicity. The three Bosnian Muslims charged in the Celebici indictment remain the only Bosnian Muslims charged in this Tribunal. If the ordinary soldiers who are of Serb ethnicity are dismissed because of the desire of the Prosecutor to concentrate on those violators of higher levels of responsibility, then in the name of equity and fairness, the indictment against Esad Landzo should necessarily be dismissed. Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you taking up this position with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have not taken up the position with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is for the Prosecutor to decide whom to prosecute and whom not to prosecute.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You're right. I think that the ball was rolling so significantly in this case that it would have been most inopportune for Ms. Arbour to have dismissed this one at the same time she dismissed the counts against the Serb indictees. But it doesn't make it any more proper or just under the circumstances. Notwithstanding the fact that the three Muslim accused in the Celebici indictment represent the only Bosnian Muslims accused in this Tribunal, Esad Landzo in 1992 was an 18-year-old prison guard with no prior military training. There is no position lower in the military hierarchy than that held by this young man. The maintenance by the Prosecutor of an indictment against Esad Landzo clearly violates Article 21(1) of the Statute of the ICTY. Article 21(1) guarantees all persons shall be equal before the International Tribunal. If there is to be equality under the statute of the ICTY, the entire indictment against Esad Landzo should be dismissed and referred back to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina for Prosecution. There is statutory support for the Prosecution of those with command responsibility. That was covered in the written final submissions, so I am not going to cover the statutory support at this time. If the indictment and charges against Esad Landzo are allowed to remain the subject of Prosecution, then Article 21 becomes moot. This Tribunal should not confuse the premise of even-handed justice with a political agenda supporting this type of indictment. Rule 67(a)(ii)(b) of the rules of procedure provide for a special defence, the Defence of diminished mental responsibility. Although this special defence is prevalent in jurisdictions based on British common law, it's unique to the war crimes arena. The Nuremberg trials utilised the premise of diminished mental responsibility. It was limited to mitigation of punishment. Although this is a special Defence provided for in the rules, there are no legal guidelines which to follow. On June 18th the Trial Chamber did rule that the burden of proving a Defence lies with the Defence and that the standard of proof is by a preponderance of the probabilities. The Trial Chamber reserved its decision on the definition of diminished mental responsibility until final judgement. Because there is no decision of the Tribunal on the legal test of diminished responsibility to be applied, preparation for presentation of evidence regarding the accused has been prejudiced pursuant to the statute.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The Defence proceeded to present evidence without a clue of what it was that must be proven in order to surmount the burden of proof which now shifted to Esad Landzo. I want to try to differentiate too. Many times throughout this trial, you heard people referring to the Prosecution's mental health expert, right or wrong? Ms. McHenry in her closing statement today referred to whether he knew right from wrong. That is not the legal standard that is to apply here. That would be lack of mental responsibility. The Defence of Esad Landzo is claiming diminished responsibility. Diminished responsibility was provided for in the Homicide Act of 1957 in Great Britain. This is the definition that we're relying on. I think it's the most prevalent in our society or in the international community which states that -- I hope we're not relying on it improvidently -- "But where a person kills or is a party to a killing of another, he shall not be convicted of murder if he was suffering from such abnormality of mind, whether arising from a condition of arrested or retarded development of mind or any inherent causes or induced by disease or injury as substantially impaired his mental responsibility for his acts and omissions in doing or being a party to the killing." The definition of abnormality of mind that is relied upon also comes from British common law. The case out of Great Britain, which is cited in my final submission says, "Abnormality of mind means a state of mind so different from that of the ordinary human beings, that the reasonable man would term it abnormal." This definition covers the mind's activity in all aspects. Not only the perception of physical acts and matters and the ability to form a rational judgement, whether the act was right or wrong, but also the ability to exercise willpower to control physical acts in accordance with that rational judgement. So, what it boils down to is whether because of the abnormality of his mind he was able to exercise his own free will. If the fact finder is satisfied by a preponderance of the probabilities that the accused was suffering for the abnormality of mind for one of the causes specified in parenthesis, the second prong of the test arises. Was the abnormality such as substantially impaired his mental responsibility for his acts in or doing or a party to the killing. This is a question of degree and essentially for the fact-finder. Without the definition, though, it was very difficult. How could the Defence know what it must prove? How could the defence advise and give legal perimeters to the experts witnesses that testified. How could the Prosecutor know how to effectively cross-examine? I hope that our reliance in this definition was not too far off base. The Defence of Esad Landzo has shown this Trial Chamber that Esad Landzo was a sickly, fragile boy to begin with. At the outbreak of the aggression against Croatia, this 18-year-old boy was subjected to the most horrific experience in a Croatian military training facility. This facility shocked the senses and moral integrity of the young students by showing violent videos depicting atrocities that were being executed upon people that the Serbs captured and culminating with live demonstrations on how to neatly torture and murder live, Serb civilians. After this brain-washing experience, the aggression came to his own home: his village, his friends and his family were under attack. The very existence of his culture was to be destroyed. All able-bodied males, even young boys, were called up for the Territorial Defence. Esad Landzo had no military experience, but he became a member of the Territorial Defence and all the young boys with no experience were stationed, not all of them, but he was stationed along with 20 others to provide security for the Celebici barracks. The Defence of Esad Landzo relies upon the autonomous decisions of three forensic psychiatrists: Dr. A.M.H. Van Leuween, Dr. Marco Laggazi, and Dr. Edward Gripon. And one clinical psychologist, Dr. Alfredo Verde, who offered evidence. Esad Landzo also relies upon the evidence elicited from the mental expert called by the prosecutor, Dr. Landy Sparr. In summary, the four mental health experts called, arrived independently at roughly the same conclusions and all agreed that he suffered from a personality disorder under Axis 1 of the DSM IV criteria and that was superimposed over an Axis 1 disorder which they called anywhere from PTSD to acute anxiety disorder to an adjustment disorder, which were all relatively the same thing. These extract personality disorders, ranging from dependant to mixed personality disorder, were all describing the same abnormality of mind. Dr. Van Leuween, who was a Dutch forensic psychiatrist initially became involved in these proceedings at the request of the registrar. Dr. Van Leuween diagnosed Esad Landzo from October 1996 until recently. He said he was suffering from a mixed personality disorder and borderline schizoid and dependant traits. He did not diagnose Mr. Landzo with PTSD in 1992 because he believed Mr. Landzo was still suffering under an ongoing trauma in 1992, so the PTSD didn't develop until later. Dr. Van Leuween explains why he cannot place Mr. Landzo's personality disorder in one category. He said that, so he has a personality disorder, but, no, it's more obvious that it's a mixed personality disorder. It is not one category. You need to use more categories to describe the realities of this person. All the mental health experts describe Mr. Landzo's dependant personality in different terms, but they all came up with the premise of the false self. The dependant personality disorder was further described by Dr. Van Leuween. Dr. Van Leuween said in Number 6: "QUESTION: Those borderline personalities, those are cognisable personality disorders, aren't they? "ANSWER: Yes. Do you see this person? How dependant he is? He told me in that camp he was under the influence of Mr. Delic." When asked by Judge Karibi-Whyte to explain the difference between a person suffering from a dependent personality disorder and the need to obey a priest or a soldier, Dr. Van Leuween explained, "Of course. There is a difference between knowing that you are obeying because the situation asked you to obey or obeying with closed eyes because you can't do anything else other than obey. And you can't do anything else other than obeying with closed eyes." Dr. Van Leuween's conclusions came up also that there was an abnormality of mind and that the abnormality of mind -- and I am going now to No. 10 what his conclusion is. That summarising his findings. What is your conclusion? "The consequence of clinical conclusion, that somebody was in a mental condition which diminished his capacity to exercise his own free will from a forensic psychiatric point of view, my advice would be to consider him to have diminished responsibility at the time of the acts." And Dr. Van Leuween went on further. Now when asked by counsel for Mr. Delic, question by Mr. Moran: "QUESTION: You've described him as a dependant personality, does that mean if there is a strong authority figure he would become dependant on that authority figure and do what that authority figure told him to do? "ANSWER: Yes." That's transcript page 14236. Alfredo Verde came up with the same results of his clinical evaluations. Alfredo Verde said that he was suffering from an abnormality of mind in 1992. That he could not control his behaviour as a result of an abnormality of mind. And that: "QUESTION: As a result of the abnormality of mind, would you say that he was in a state of diminished mental capacity? "ANSWER: Yeah. "QUESTION: In Celebici in 1992? "ANSWER: Yeah." Transcript, 14403. When questioned by Judge Karibi-Whyte about the abnormality of mind, Dr. Verde explained, "And he was not such a capacity, but he tends to put on, to wear the clothes of others. It's rather like an animal. A chameleon. Yes, changing colours according to the environment." Dr. Lagazzi arrived at the same conclusions, a forensic psychiatric from Genoa, Italy, he was called here at the request of the Prosecution in 1996. He has been evaluating Mr. Landzo over that period. No. 12. Dr. Lagazzi said he clearly fits under the DSM IV category of mixed personality disorder. When you begin with these various personality disorders and then you overlay these with PTSD, you result in a severely enhanced condition of PTSD. When Judge Karibi-Whyte asked Dr. Lagazzi to relate the personality disorder to the mental ability of the accused person to commit offences against which he is charged and the extent to what he is responsible,

utterances.speaker: DR. LAGAZZI REPLIED
utterances.text: "So, what I have done is to assess the individual. And I believe that this kind of personality in specific circumstances of authority may lead to the acceptance of an order and lead, in turn, to certain attitudes without using one's own free choice." In other words, where free will is absent. And Dr. Lagazzi continued, "In other words, Mr. Landzo had a clinical condition and it was probable on the basis of that condition that when he received very specific orders, he would then act in a non-free manner." Transcript 14551 through 552. He also went on to describe the "Zelig" movie by Woody Allen. He gave you the instruction or the example of the red shoes where normality spills over into abnormality. He also came to the same conclusions as the other ones. No. 14. When he was asked whether he was suffering from an abnormality of mind in 1992, the answer was "yes." When asked if this abnormality of mind influenced his ability to control his behaviour in the setting as a guard in Celebici in 1992, the answer: "There is a probability that it did influence his behaviour." When asked whether he suffered from lack of free will in 1992, the answer was: "I can tell you that this lack of free will was in all likelihood to be found at the time he was in Celebici." Dr. Lagazzi continued, No. 15. "To show why Esad Landzo could not exercise his own free will." "So you believe this man was incapable of exercising free will over a period of say two or three months in 1992, in the summer?" "ANSWER: Sorry, but let me once again go to the logical sequence of the work which I have gotten into. I do have clinical findings to prove a pathological personality disorder. I have a legal definition which I have been given, which refers to abnormality personality as a possible cause for diminished responsibility. And this led me to say, if you combine these two elements, we could say that there is a probability that there is diminished responsibility." I am not going to go into detail because of the time constraints. Dr. Gripon, who was an American forensic psychiatrist came up with the very same conclusions that all the other forensic psychiatrists came up with and I have the exact quotes set out in the final submission. And then we came to the Prosecutor's expert, Dr. Landy Sparr. Dr. Sparr, when I questioned him about what standard he used to come up with his opinions in his report, he told us four different standards and they were all of his own creation. None were legally acceptable standards that he used to come up with his opinion. So all the conclusions that are asserted in his report and testimony should be disregarded and be considered baseless. That too is in the final submission. I would like to go to the indictment. Since I am probably running out of time, I would like to summarise -- pardon? Eight minutes. Of course, Mr. Landzo testified and we believe that the best testimony, the best evidence in this case is the testimony of Mr. Landzo. It took a lot of courage to come here and testify. And he admitted that he participated in the beating of Scepo Gotovac. He told us about the circumstances, how he was handed a piece of paper out of the window by Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delic, saying that they wanted this man to come out with his feet first because someone else had come there and told them they had a vendetta against this man. Well, we believe that he should be found not guilty of those counts in the indictment because he was suffering from such diminished mental capacity that rendered his judgement diminished responsibility for the acts at that time. Simo Jovanovic. Mr. Landzo testified that, yes, he called Simo Jovanovic out. That the guards from Idbar had come there and they took him over into the workshop and they beat him and he returned him back to the hangar 20 minutes later. And, yes, he did say that Mr. Simo Jovanovic more than likely died from the beating that he received that evening. But, most of all, we come to Mr. Bosko Samoukovic, who was an elderly man, who was just one of the six or seven people that Mr. Landzo hit in the hangar when he returned on July 12th, 1992. In July 12th, I can't go through all of the testimony, but, you know, he had just come from the scene of the most brutal murder of the person who had been his father figure for the previous few years, Ibro, who lived above him and seen how he had been mutilated, his body destroyed and mutilated. He went back, and because he was in such a diminished mental state, that he couldn't control his actions and he did admit to going in and hitting this man. One thing that the Prosecution hasn't proven, Mr. Landzo called the nurse immediately to help this man when he saw that he was seriously injured. He took him straight to the infirmary. He ordered the doctors to make him well. Now a murderer doesn't do that. That doesn't make sense. There was no intent on Mr. Landzo's part to murder Mr. Samoukovic. And that would be very hard stretched for the Prosecutor to say that there was. Mr. Susic, the fourth allegation of murder against Mr. Landzo. Mr. Landzo said, yes, he did go with the other guards to put him in Tunnel 9. And as he did put him in Tunnel 9, he did push him. Mr. Susic, he was beaten. But Mr. Landzo did not beat him during the times that ended up resulting in his death. Of course there are four allegations of torture against Mr. Landzo. I promise, Judge Jan, and your Honourable Court that I will come up with the definition of torture when we come back tomorrow. But the definition of torture as submitted by the Prosecution is clearly too broad. We have Witness M. Witness M, Mr. Landzo admitted -- can you put No. 27 on, please? Mr. Landzo's testimony was that, yes, he did burn Witness M. Yes, he did participate in the beatings of Witness M. He did it with Hazim Delic watching him and he was ordered to do so. Witness N, he also says that he remembers Witness N being beaten by the HOS. He doesn't remember Mirko Babic. He doesn't remember Mirko -- no, Mirko Djordjic he does remember. No, he doesn't remember Mirko Djordjic. Nedeljko Draganic, who is the charge of great suffering, he knew him from school. He said he came in as Nedeljko Draganic was being beaten over in the other hangar. And, yes, when he was told to put him back in the hangar, he kicked him or hit him and tried to get him up and he did put him back in the hangar. But he did not do the torturous allegations that are in Counts 36 and 37. And, of course, it would be ludicrous to hold a young guard, 18 years-old, responsible for the inhuman conditions at the camp. The fact is, Esad Landzo had no authority to change any of the conditions in the camp. And he had no command responsibility. So the allegations of inhumane conditions in Count 46 and 47 should be dismissed against Esad Landzo. I want to address the lack of credibility of the Prosecution witnesses one more time. They were all allowed to come here and tell their story. Each Prosecutor that testified here had six years, five to six years to get their stories together. They went to a testifying seminar in Temisoara (Phoen), Romania. They are now not able to separate what they heard in those seminars. What it is they've talked to each other about over those six years and what it is that they actually remember or heard themselves. Each Prosecution witness testified that Esad Landzo was the guard posted at the door of Hangar No. 6, the building where the majority of the detainees were held. His was the only name they knew. When they wanted to contact the outside world, they shouted Landzo, Zenga, in order to make any kind of communications. He carried messages, solved problems and answered their calls. He was the name that they recognised, the name they knew. He is the guard that's here, present. If I might conclude, in a multi-defendant trial, especially one with the underpinnings of national integrity, national pride and political warfare still in the forefront, the decision to testify becomes a matter of life or death and of national dignity. Esad Landzo chose at the risk of the threat of his home, his family and himself to come before this tribunal and testify. This was a courageous decision. Esad Landzo wished to present the best Defence that he could to the allegations by the prosecutor. But he was inhibited and prevented from doing so by intimidation and interference with the witnesses who previously agreed to come forward and speak the truth. There is no doubt that terrible acts occurred in the camp during the summer of 1992. These regrettable acts can now be defined and viewed as a result of the aggression and the atmosphere of fear and panic that was forced upon the people of the Konjic Municipality. Whatever the motivation, our goals in this International Tribunal are to understand what the causes were in 1992. An attempt to prevent a recurrence of such events, the entire scheme of crimes against humanity must, if it is to have moral vigour, to maintain the support of world opinion, must be designed to attack and punish command responsibility. It is aimed at the destruction of any military or authoritarian command structure, which breeds, nurtures, creates or encourages savagery, mayhem and violates the common notions of human dignity. To focus the light of world opinion upon a prison guard, denigrates the process. The punishment of a hapless 19-year-old caught up in the midst of a confusing conflict, a conflict which literally came to his doorstep, is such a simplistic and unfair solution, it defames the original noble intent of the framers of the law. In our world, among those people who share the notion of civility and common decency, there is a shared perception that those who conceive, plan and execute crimes against humanity should be caught and punished. From such high convictions, this Tribunal draws its force. Let it not be squandered in the pursuit of common soldiers and prison guards. Such actions diminish the moral authority from which world justice springs. Notwithstanding the common legal arguments put forth by all of the accused in the Celebici case, Esad Landzo presented strong and compelling evidence that while stationed as a guard in the Celebici barracks, he existed in a state of diminished mental capacity, legally resulting in a state of diminished mental responsibility. The burden of proof was merely by a preponderance of the probabilities. This burden of proof has most assuredly been surmounted by the consistent testimony of four independent health experts, each of whom testified that Esad Landzo should be found to have diminished mental responsibility for his actions in 1992. Once again I want to thank this Tribunal. I really appreciate my participation in this trial. On behalf of Esad Landzo, I want to say that we have met our burden of proof and this Honourable Trial Chamber should return a verdict of not guilty to the counts in the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it's 5.30 now, we shall adjourn until tomorrow for the Prosecution to continue for any possible rebuttal it has. So the Trial Chamber will now rise.
